SUPERVISION  AND  CONTROL
The Supervisory Board has monitored the Management Board on the basis of written and verbal
reporting and performed the duties for which it is responsible in accordance with applicable
statutes. The Supervisory Board was informed of important matters about J.P. Morgan SE’s
financial result, the business development, the capital and liquidity situation as well as the risk
management profile. This has been done during the meetings of the Supervisory Board and its
committees as well as by means of written and oral ad-hoc reporting.

In  2024, the Supervisory Board continued to welcome new members to both the Management
and Supervisory Boards, whilst maintaining effective oversight of the Bank’s risk profile and
financial results. Geopolitical events in Europe and around the world remain the focus, which will
intensify in 2025, but the highly diversified business activities of the Bank and low risk taking
provide significant resiliency. More normal levels of interest rates, compared to the historic lows
in Europe, aided profitability in 2024. More uncertain markets and political outlooks can provide
significant contributions to business growth as clients seek advice, market access and financing.
The Supervisory Board continues to monitor these developments as well as regulatory matters
to ensure a strong and effective governance framework.

PERSONNEL  CHANGE S  IN  THE  MANAGEMENT  B OA R D
Jessica Kaffrén joined J.P.  Morgan  SE on January 2  ,  2024 as the new Head of Operations, Out  -
sourcing and Technology, and on July 1  , 2024 as the member of the Management Board, which
was previously covered on an interim basis by Nicholas Conron (Outsourcing) and Burkhard
Kübel-Sorger (Operations and Technology), following the departure of Cindyrella Amistadi on
March   15,  2023. Furthermore, Burkhard Kübel-Sorger departed J.P.  Morgan  SE end of June
2024. David Fellowes-Freeman was appointed as CFo with effect from August  1,  2024. Claudia
Tarantino was appointed as Chief Compliance Officer with effect from January 1  , 2025 and Daniel
Llano Manibardo was appointed with effect from April 1  , 2025 as a member of the Management
Board. As of May 20,  2025 the Management Board comprises eight members.

PERSONNEL  CHANGE S  IN  THE  S U P E RV I S O RY  B OA R D
Susan Dean resigned from the Supervisory Board with effect from end of January 2024. Frank
Pearn and Ann Doherty were appointed as Supervisory Board members with effect from March 1,
2024 to fill the vacancies. Peter Augsten (employee representative) succeeded Thomas Freise,
who resigned from the Supervisory Board with effect from June 30,  2024, with effect as from
July 1, 2024. Paul Uminski resigned with effect from December 31,  2024 and Thomas Schulz was
appointed with effect from January 1  , 2025. Wanda Eriksen resigned with effect from March   15,
2025 and Natasha Banse was appointed with effect from March 16,  2025.

# Autism by the Numbers: 2023 Annual Report

2023 Annual Report
*   [Autism by the Numbers](https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-speaks-autism-numbers)
*   [State Summaries](https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-numbers-state-summaries)
*   [2025 Annual Report](https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-numbers-2025-annual-report)
*   2023 Annual Report

[_**Download a PDF of the full executive summary**_](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/ABN_Executive_Summary_2023.pdf)

[![Image 12: Screenshot of Autism by the Numbers Annual Report with a link to download the full report](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_download%20report.png?itok=SdYnd2Nj)](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/ABN_Annual_Report_2023.pdf)

The autistic community experiences disparities in multiple areas, including education, healthcare and employment. Current autism data and the way it is presented does not provide an accurate sense of the lived experience of people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in the U.S. For the first time, Autism by the Numbers offers accessible, state-level information that will enable autistic individuals and their families to make meaningful life decisions.

Autism by the Numbers, created by Autism Speaks in collaboration with the [National Autism Data Center at Drexel University](https://nationalautismdatacenter.org/ "nationalautismdatacenter.org"), has the potential to transform the way we understand and meet the needs of autistic individuals and their families. This central, authoritative hub of reliable data about people with autism will allow insight into the strengths and weaknesses of systems that exist to improve health, education, employment and advocacy. The Autism by the Numbers [Annual Report](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/ABN_Annual_Report_2023.pdf) and [Dashboard](https://nationalautismdatacenter.org/autism-by-the-numbers/) can also be used to support the creation of precision public health programs specific to the diverse needs of the autistic community.

![Image 13: Callout saying unmet needs remain across the life span of autistic individuals](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_fullscreen_width/public/ABN_unmet%20needs.png?itok=4F5d-LfE)

## Childhood early intervention & diagnosis

Autism by the Numbers data show that **1 in 35 children aged 3-17 in the U.S. are diagnosed with ASD**. These numbers are closely aligned with the CDC prevalence rate of 1 in 36 children aged 8.

**On average, Autism by the Numbers data show that autistic children receive intervention services and support prior to being diagnosed.**

![Image 14: 1 in 35 children aged 3-17 are diagnosed with ASD](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_1%20in%2035%20diagnosis.png?itok=cJYUQxjc)

*   This demonstrates that screening processes have been somewhat effective.
*   However, there is a need for better screening tools that allow us to identify and support underdiagnosed groups.
*   Girls and people with more complex autism symptoms are often diagnosed later,with the **average age of diagnosis for girls at 5.6 years**.

**Prior research has proven that intervention services are crucial, and earlier is better to make a meaningful impact.**

![Image 15: Infographic saying average age of first intervention ranges from 3.7 to 7.2 years across states](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small/public/ABN_age%20of%20intervention.png?itok=2D41W8GG)

*   Research shows that autism can be reliably diagnosed by age 2, though the **average age of diagnosis is age 5**.
*   Early diagnosis and intervention can have a positive lifelong impact on people with autism. Studies show that interventions started before age 4 may improve cognition,language, daily living skills and social skills.
*   Earlier diagnosis makes it easier to map out a path for the future, including planning for special education services and other public programs.

**Autism by the Numbers data also show variation between states in access to diagnosis and early intervention.**

![Image 16: Infographic showing average age of intervention and diagnosis in the U.S.](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_age%20of%20intervention%20%26%20diagnosis.png?itok=SscWp14q)

*   **Average age of first intervention ranges from 3.7 to 7.2 years** of age across states.
*   Average age of diagnosis ranges from 3.6 years to 7.6 years across states.
*   Delaware and Kentucky have the youngest age of first intervention, at 3.7 years in each state.
*   Oklahoma (5.3 years), Mississippi (5.5 years), Ohio (5.6 years), North Dakota(6.0 years) and West Virginia (7.2 years) show an average age of intervention above the national average, indicating a possible need to improve screening processes or access to intervention services.

More in-depth research is needed to understand why some states are able to effectively screen for ASD and provide early intervention services, while others experience significant delays in care.

![Image 17: Bar graph showing average age of first intervention by state in the U.S.](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_fullscreen_width/public/ABN_age%20of%20intervention%20by%20state.png?itok=N48nVB90)

**Autism by the Numbers has the power to bring vital data to light that can be used for advocacy and**  
**policy changes to improve screening and cut down on delays to services.**

*   State-specific data could allow states to better allocate resources and explore ways to improve screening and increase access to services and supports.
*   The data can also benefit families, improving awareness of and access to services and support programs in their state.

## Healthcare costs

Children with autism have a higher rate of mental and physical health concerns that may require more healthcare services, such as provider visits and medications – and therefore, higher expenses.

The downside of not having accurate or reliable data about the autistic community is that it prevents Medicaid and other insurers from providing ample resources. Autism by the Numbers can help draw a more complete picture of the amount and kinds of coverage needed to properly care for autistic individuals. Additional healthcare needs experienced by autistic children underscore the importance of ensuring they have reliable healthcare coverage.

**Nationally, most autistic children have some kind of coverage through Medicaid, one of the main**  
**insurance providers.**

*   Some states offer Medicaid waivers for all people with intellectual or developmental disabilities, while others have special waivers specifically for autism.
*   While autism waivers exist, there can be delays and other barriers preventing easy access to them.

![Image 18: Map of states with autism-specific Medicaid waivers](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_large_width/public/ABN_autism-specific%20waivers%20map.png?itok=6fZzipw5)

**Autism by the Numbers data explores the costs of common services related to autism.**

*   While healthcare costs are generally higher for autistic children, care is usually paid for by public or private insurance.
*   We do not have an accurate sense of the out-of-pocket healthcare costs of autistic individuals and their families, but the data indicate that these costs vary greatly by state.

![Image 19: Chart of healthcare costs organized by service category](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_large_width/public/ABN_healthcare%20costs.png?itok=1wxdFhZl)

## Transitioning out of High School

Many people with autism receive services through their school systems but lose access to those services and vital supports upon leaving high school. Without continuity of services,it can be more difficult for autistic adults to obtain employment, continue their education or live independently, which could potentially impact their future.

![Image 20: Infographic showing high school graduation rates among autistic students in special education](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_graduation%20rates.png?itok=XA1Fz0uo)

**Autism by the Numbers data shows the outcomes for autistic students**  
**who receive special education services.**

*   Nationally, 10% of students in special education programs receive special education services for autism. Not all autistic students qualify for special education, so there may be students who lack necessary support in school.
*   **73.6% of autistic students receiving special education graduate with a high school diploma** and another 19.3% finish with certificates.
*   **8.1% drop out of high school**, though we don’t know why.

**Vocational Rehabilitation (VR) training and services provide an effective pathway to preparing autistic adolescents and teens for employment.**

![Image 21: Infographic saying that 50% of autistic youth and young adults receive VR services](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small/public/ABN_VR%20services.png?itok=TLnzAcSm)

*   Autistic students receive VR services at a lower rate than students with other disabilities, and transition-age autistic adults have lower rates of employment than those with other disabilities.
*   On average, **50% of autistic youth and young adults receive VR services**. This ranges from 10% in New Jersey to 77% in Oklahoma.
*   Among those who received VR services in high school, **60% had a job when they left school**. This range was from a low of 32% in Washington, D.C. to a high of 76%in Nebraska.

**There is still work to be done to increase the number of autistic students who graduate high school and go on to find employment.We need research to further explore these questions:**

![Image 22: Infographic saying that 40% of young adults with autism who receive VR do not find employment after high school](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_VR%20outcomes.png?itok=LrPAybGk)

*   What are the longitudinal employment trends for autistic individuals?
*   Why is the dropout rate so high, and how can we better support autistic students to have a positive experience in school?
*   How many autistic young adults did not receive VR training, and why? How can we improve this number?
*   How can we better serve students in pursuing education or employment after high school?

The challenges autistic people experience while transitioning out of school and into adult life are an important area of focus for Autism Speaks. As the Autism by the Numbers Dashboard evolves, it will include more attention to and information about this life step.

![Image 23: Infographic saying there are 5.4 million autistic adults in the US](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small/public/ABN_autistic%20adults.png?itok=whoXvoXX)

## Adults and aging with autism

There is a pressing need to put systems in place to care for the approximately 5.4 million adults with autism in the U.S. While there is limited research and information on aging in autism,expanding our knowledge around this topic is of vital importance.

**Currently, knowledge of aging in autism suggests that:**

![Image 24: Infographic saying no official clinical practice guidelines focus on the care of autistic adults](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_clinical%20practice.png?itok=_p-70qdC)

*   The population of autistic adults in the U.S. is growing.
*   Autistic adults need specific support programs and appropriate care.
*   Adults with autism continue to have greater medical needs and lifetime healthcare costs.
*   We lack a full understanding of the needs of autistic adults and how to care for them.
*   There are currently no official practice guidelines or standards of care for treating autistic adults.

Additional research, conducted in close partnership with autistic individuals, can eventually  
lead to the creation of practice guidelines that will advance healthcare for autistic adults.

## The future

Annual updates to the Autism by the Numbers Dashboard will continue to track and expand data on the most pressing areas of concern for autistic people and their families, including but not limited to mental and physical health and food security across the lifespan.

Autistic people interact with multiple systems. Linking, or connecting, data sources can help us to better understand the day-to-day experiences of the autistic community. For example, linking survey data with administrative claims data can provide us with a fuller picture of the needs of autistic people across systems. In the future, we plan to conduct data linkages and provide important indicators back to the community.

![Image 25: Callout saying Autism by the Numbers has the ability to make a positive impact in the lives of the autistic community](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_fullscreen_width/public/ABN_callout.png?itok=JazkJ86p)

# Autism by the Numbers: 2023 Annual Report

2023 Annual Report
*   [Autism by the Numbers](https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-speaks-autism-numbers)
*   [State Summaries](https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-numbers-state-summaries)
*   [2025 Annual Report](https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-numbers-2025-annual-report)
*   2023 Annual Report

[_**Download a PDF of the full executive summary**_](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/ABN_Executive_Summary_2023.pdf)

[![Image 12: Screenshot of Autism by the Numbers Annual Report with a link to download the full report](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_download%20report.png?itok=SdYnd2Nj)](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/ABN_Annual_Report_2023.pdf)

The autistic community experiences disparities in multiple areas, including education, healthcare and employment. Current autism data and the way it is presented does not provide an accurate sense of the lived experience of people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in the U.S. For the first time, Autism by the Numbers offers accessible, state-level information that will enable autistic individuals and their families to make meaningful life decisions.

Autism by the Numbers, created by Autism Speaks in collaboration with the [National Autism Data Center at Drexel University](https://nationalautismdatacenter.org/ "nationalautismdatacenter.org"), has the potential to transform the way we understand and meet the needs of autistic individuals and their families. This central, authoritative hub of reliable data about people with autism will allow insight into the strengths and weaknesses of systems that exist to improve health, education, employment and advocacy. The Autism by the Numbers [Annual Report](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/ABN_Annual_Report_2023.pdf) and [Dashboard](https://nationalautismdatacenter.org/autism-by-the-numbers/) can also be used to support the creation of precision public health programs specific to the diverse needs of the autistic community.

![Image 13: Callout saying unmet needs remain across the life span of autistic individuals](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_fullscreen_width/public/ABN_unmet%20needs.png?itok=4F5d-LfE)

## Childhood early intervention & diagnosis

Autism by the Numbers data show that **1 in 35 children aged 3-17 in the U.S. are diagnosed with ASD**. These numbers are closely aligned with the CDC prevalence rate of 1 in 36 children aged 8.

**On average, Autism by the Numbers data show that autistic children receive intervention services and support prior to being diagnosed.**

![Image 14: 1 in 35 children aged 3-17 are diagnosed with ASD](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_1%20in%2035%20diagnosis.png?itok=cJYUQxjc)

*   This demonstrates that screening processes have been somewhat effective.
*   However, there is a need for better screening tools that allow us to identify and support underdiagnosed groups.
*   Girls and people with more complex autism symptoms are often diagnosed later,with the **average age of diagnosis for girls at 5.6 years**.

**Prior research has proven that intervention services are crucial, and earlier is better to make a meaningful impact.**

![Image 15: Infographic saying average age of first intervention ranges from 3.7 to 7.2 years across states](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small/public/ABN_age%20of%20intervention.png?itok=2D41W8GG)

*   Research shows that autism can be reliably diagnosed by age 2, though the **average age of diagnosis is age 5**.
*   Early diagnosis and intervention can have a positive lifelong impact on people with autism. Studies show that interventions started before age 4 may improve cognition,language, daily living skills and social skills.
*   Earlier diagnosis makes it easier to map out a path for the future, including planning for special education services and other public programs.

**Autism by the Numbers data also show variation between states in access to diagnosis and early intervention.**

![Image 16: Infographic showing average age of intervention and diagnosis in the U.S.](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_age%20of%20intervention%20%26%20diagnosis.png?itok=SscWp14q)

*   **Average age of first intervention ranges from 3.7 to 7.2 years** of age across states.
*   Average age of diagnosis ranges from 3.6 years to 7.6 years across states.
*   Delaware and Kentucky have the youngest age of first intervention, at 3.7 years in each state.
*   Oklahoma (5.3 years), Mississippi (5.5 years), Ohio (5.6 years), North Dakota(6.0 years) and West Virginia (7.2 years) show an average age of intervention above the national average, indicating a possible need to improve screening processes or access to intervention services.

More in-depth research is needed to understand why some states are able to effectively screen for ASD and provide early intervention services, while others experience significant delays in care.

![Image 17: Bar graph showing average age of first intervention by state in the U.S.](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_fullscreen_width/public/ABN_age%20of%20intervention%20by%20state.png?itok=N48nVB90)

**Autism by the Numbers has the power to bring vital data to light that can be used for advocacy and**  
**policy changes to improve screening and cut down on delays to services.**

*   State-specific data could allow states to better allocate resources and explore ways to improve screening and increase access to services and supports.
*   The data can also benefit families, improving awareness of and access to services and support programs in their state.

## Healthcare costs

Children with autism have a higher rate of mental and physical health concerns that may require more healthcare services, such as provider visits and medications – and therefore, higher expenses.

The downside of not having accurate or reliable data about the autistic community is that it prevents Medicaid and other insurers from providing ample resources. Autism by the Numbers can help draw a more complete picture of the amount and kinds of coverage needed to properly care for autistic individuals. Additional healthcare needs experienced by autistic children underscore the importance of ensuring they have reliable healthcare coverage.

**Nationally, most autistic children have some kind of coverage through Medicaid, one of the main**  
**insurance providers.**

*   Some states offer Medicaid waivers for all people with intellectual or developmental disabilities, while others have special waivers specifically for autism.
*   While autism waivers exist, there can be delays and other barriers preventing easy access to them.

![Image 18: Map of states with autism-specific Medicaid waivers](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_large_width/public/ABN_autism-specific%20waivers%20map.png?itok=6fZzipw5)

**Autism by the Numbers data explores the costs of common services related to autism.**

*   While healthcare costs are generally higher for autistic children, care is usually paid for by public or private insurance.
*   We do not have an accurate sense of the out-of-pocket healthcare costs of autistic individuals and their families, but the data indicate that these costs vary greatly by state.

![Image 19: Chart of healthcare costs organized by service category](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_large_width/public/ABN_healthcare%20costs.png?itok=1wxdFhZl)

## Transitioning out of High School

Many people with autism receive services through their school systems but lose access to those services and vital supports upon leaving high school. Without continuity of services,it can be more difficult for autistic adults to obtain employment, continue their education or live independently, which could potentially impact their future.

![Image 20: Infographic showing high school graduation rates among autistic students in special education](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_graduation%20rates.png?itok=XA1Fz0uo)

**Autism by the Numbers data shows the outcomes for autistic students**  
**who receive special education services.**

*   Nationally, 10% of students in special education programs receive special education services for autism. Not all autistic students qualify for special education, so there may be students who lack necessary support in school.
*   **73.6% of autistic students receiving special education graduate with a high school diploma** and another 19.3% finish with certificates.
*   **8.1% drop out of high school**, though we don’t know why.

**Vocational Rehabilitation (VR) training and services provide an effective pathway to preparing autistic adolescents and teens for employment.**

![Image 21: Infographic saying that 50% of autistic youth and young adults receive VR services](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small/public/ABN_VR%20services.png?itok=TLnzAcSm)

*   Autistic students receive VR services at a lower rate than students with other disabilities, and transition-age autistic adults have lower rates of employment than those with other disabilities.
*   On average, **50% of autistic youth and young adults receive VR services**. This ranges from 10% in New Jersey to 77% in Oklahoma.
*   Among those who received VR services in high school, **60% had a job when they left school**. This range was from a low of 32% in Washington, D.C. to a high of 76%in Nebraska.

**There is still work to be done to increase the number of autistic students who graduate high school and go on to find employment.We need research to further explore these questions:**

![Image 22: Infographic saying that 40% of young adults with autism who receive VR do not find employment after high school](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_VR%20outcomes.png?itok=LrPAybGk)

*   What are the longitudinal employment trends for autistic individuals?
*   Why is the dropout rate so high, and how can we better support autistic students to have a positive experience in school?
*   How many autistic young adults did not receive VR training, and why? How can we improve this number?
*   How can we better serve students in pursuing education or employment after high school?

The challenges autistic people experience while transitioning out of school and into adult life are an important area of focus for Autism Speaks. As the Autism by the Numbers Dashboard evolves, it will include more attention to and information about this life step.

![Image 23: Infographic saying there are 5.4 million autistic adults in the US](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small/public/ABN_autistic%20adults.png?itok=whoXvoXX)

## Adults and aging with autism

There is a pressing need to put systems in place to care for the approximately 5.4 million adults with autism in the U.S. While there is limited research and information on aging in autism,expanding our knowledge around this topic is of vital importance.

**Currently, knowledge of aging in autism suggests that:**

![Image 24: Infographic saying no official clinical practice guidelines focus on the care of autistic adults](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_small_width/public/ABN_clinical%20practice.png?itok=_p-70qdC)

*   The population of autistic adults in the U.S. is growing.
*   Autistic adults need specific support programs and appropriate care.
*   Adults with autism continue to have greater medical needs and lifetime healthcare costs.
*   We lack a full understanding of the needs of autistic adults and how to care for them.
*   There are currently no official practice guidelines or standards of care for treating autistic adults.

Additional research, conducted in close partnership with autistic individuals, can eventually  
lead to the creation of practice guidelines that will advance healthcare for autistic adults.

## The future

Annual updates to the Autism by the Numbers Dashboard will continue to track and expand data on the most pressing areas of concern for autistic people and their families, including but not limited to mental and physical health and food security across the lifespan.

Autistic people interact with multiple systems. Linking, or connecting, data sources can help us to better understand the day-to-day experiences of the autistic community. For example, linking survey data with administrative claims data can provide us with a fuller picture of the needs of autistic people across systems. In the future, we plan to conduct data linkages and provide important indicators back to the community.

![Image 25: Callout saying Autism by the Numbers has the ability to make a positive impact in the lives of the autistic community](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_fullscreen_width/public/ABN_callout.png?itok=JazkJ86p)

# Autism Through the Years: How Understanding Has Evolved Over Two Decades

![Image 4](https://autismcenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/History-of-Autism-Prevalence-Rates_2025.png)

Thanks to a dedicated and supportive community, SARRC has spent over two decades advancing the understanding and treatment of autism. But what did the autism landscape look like back in 1997? We asked members of SARRC’s research team to reflect on those early days. Here’s a glimpse of how far we’ve come since then.

**What is the prevalence of autism among children in the United States?**

In 1997, autism was on the rise, and so were people’s concerns, yet there were no dedicated efforts to monitor prevalence rates. In 1995, rough estimates suggested that 1 in 500 children were likely to be diagnosed with autism. In the year 2000, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) began carefully tracking prevalence rates through the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network. Today, the CDC reports that 1 in 31 children has been identified with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

**What is the average age children are receiving an autism diagnosis?**

The estimated average age of diagnosis in the U.S. was 4 years, 4 months in 1997. While parental concerns were noted in earlier development, it was more common for children to be identified and diagnosed upon reaching school age. As of 2025, the CDC reports that the average age of diagnosis in the U.S. is 3 years, 11 months. However, research has shown that a reliable diagnosis of autism can be made as early as 2 years old.

**What does the existing body of scientific research say about what factors are driving rising autism rates?**

One of the most significant shifts occurred in 2013 with the release of the DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders), the diagnostic manual used by professionals to identify mental and developmental conditions. This revision consolidated several previously separate diagnoses, such as autistic disorder, Asperger’s disorder, and Pervasive Developmental Disorder-Not Otherwise Specified (PDD-NOS) — into a single diagnosis: autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This broadened the diagnostic criteria, resulting in more individuals falling under the ASD umbrella compared to the earlier DSM-IV framework.

At the same time, growing public awareness, evolving treatment approaches, and increased visibility of children with autism in public education settings have all contributed to higher recognition and diagnosis rates. As people become more familiar with the signs of autism, it’s more likely that individuals who may have been missed in the past are now being identified.

When looking at reported prevalence over time, earlier estimates have increased, but recent data from the CDC have shown a relatively stable pattern, hovering around 1 in 44, 1 in 36, and 1 in 31 in the last few reports. These smaller incremental changes, as opposed to sharp spikes in increases, suggest the effect of the diagnostic changes is leveling off, and we’re approaching a more accurate and consistent understanding of autism prevalence in the general population.

**What does existing research say about what causes autism?**

There’s no solid scientific evidence that points to a single cause for autism. Instead, research shows that autism is a complex condition with many different contributing factors.

These can range from genetic influences to environmental ones — or most likely, a mix of both. In fact, scientists have found links between autism and hundreds of different genes, which underscores just how multifaceted it is.

Autism isn’t something that can be “cured,” but it is best considered an alternate developmental pathway, where some are much more profoundly impaired than others. Autism is not a disease, so there is no cure. Instead, the best strategy is intervention that helps autistic individuals learn and develop skills that lead to their personal, optimal level of independence.

**Is there any research into whether environmental factors are linked to rising autism rates?**

Scientists have explored a variety of environmental toxins, none of which have been firmly implicated as a clearly linked cause that explains all — or even a significant minority — of why people have autism. There have been many changes in our environment over the past three decades that may be correlated with the rising rates of autism, from air pollution and rising carbon dioxide in our atmosphere to the use of technology and cell phones. But as we were all taught in basic high school science, correlation does not imply causation. Forgetting that basic tenet of science can lead to a significant waste of precious resources that could be better directed toward more legitimate scientific endeavors.

**What are the expected outcomes for adults with autism?**

When SARRC was founded in 1997, very little was known about the outcomes for adults with autism. The prevalence of autism was continually increasing, but long-term expectations were unclear. While many large care facilities closed in the 1980s, it was not uncommon for institutionalization to be suggested as part of the care of people with autism. Children who were diagnosed in 1997 are young adults now, and places like SARRC are working to build and shape inclusive employment and educational opportunities. According to a 2017 National Autism Indicators Report, only 14 percent of adults with autism had a job for pay outside of the home within the first two years after leaving high school. Over the next decade, it is estimated that up to 1 million youth with autism will transition to adulthood and may be seeking employment.

**What factors, if any, influence how often boys vs. girls are diagnosed with autism?**

Studies consistently find higher rates of autism in boys than girls. Currently, the male-to-female ratio for autism is estimated to be 3:1. This gender gap is narrowing (it used to be 4:1 or even slightly larger), and improvements in identifying autism in girls have led to research aiming to understand the disparity and to determine whether or not girls are being underdiagnosed. While the results are not yet definitive, the body of research that is starting to emerge is promising for early diagnosis in females, and that is invaluable. However, the gender gap is still prominent, which implicates genetics as the most likely cause of autism.

Early research on autism planted a seed for a male stereotype of the disorder and led to diagnostic procedures being largely male-biased, using male norms. In reality, females often present differently. They may have fewer repetitive behaviors, and their restricted interests may be more socially acceptable and therefore go unnoticed. They may also have a more socially appropriate communication style. With these social camouflaging traits, females are more likely to appear as if they are fitting in when they’re young, so it doesn’t raise a flag.

Common stereotypes and gendered expectations about females in general may help fuel the possibility of underdiagnosing girls. Females with autism often demonstrate some appropriate social skills. They may have good eye contact, develop language and gestures on time, and demonstrate social motivation, which can be misleading to parents and pediatricians. However, they may show subtle social differences, like making odd or too many social initiations, misreading social cues, and engaging in repetitive speech.

**How have diagnostic criteria changed in the past 20 years?**

Autistic disorder, Asperger’s disorder, and Pervasive Developmental Disorder (PDD) were three distinct developmental disorders with different diagnostic criteria, namely a lack of significant language delay in individuals with Asperger’s and an atypical onset or atypical presentation of autism associated with PDD. The division between these three developmental disorders often causes issues related to access to services as well as general care.

In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) newly identified autism as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), folding all subcategories of the condition into one umbrella diagnosis. Autistic disorder, Asperger’s disorder, and PDD are no longer considered separate conditions.

Since our founding, SARRC has remained dedicated to conducting innovative research, providing evidence-based practices, disseminating effective training, and building inclusive communities for individuals with autism and their families.

# Autism Through the Years: How Understanding Has Evolved Over Two Decades

![Image 4](https://autismcenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/History-of-Autism-Prevalence-Rates_2025.png)

Thanks to a dedicated and supportive community, SARRC has spent over two decades advancing the understanding and treatment of autism. But what did the autism landscape look like back in 1997? We asked members of SARRC’s research team to reflect on those early days. Here’s a glimpse of how far we’ve come since then.

**What is the prevalence of autism among children in the United States?**

In 1997, autism was on the rise, and so were people’s concerns, yet there were no dedicated efforts to monitor prevalence rates. In 1995, rough estimates suggested that 1 in 500 children were likely to be diagnosed with autism. In the year 2000, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) began carefully tracking prevalence rates through the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network. Today, the CDC reports that 1 in 31 children has been identified with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

**What is the average age children are receiving an autism diagnosis?**

The estimated average age of diagnosis in the U.S. was 4 years, 4 months in 1997. While parental concerns were noted in earlier development, it was more common for children to be identified and diagnosed upon reaching school age. As of 2025, the CDC reports that the average age of diagnosis in the U.S. is 3 years, 11 months. However, research has shown that a reliable diagnosis of autism can be made as early as 2 years old.

**What does the existing body of scientific research say about what factors are driving rising autism rates?**

One of the most significant shifts occurred in 2013 with the release of the DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders), the diagnostic manual used by professionals to identify mental and developmental conditions. This revision consolidated several previously separate diagnoses, such as autistic disorder, Asperger’s disorder, and Pervasive Developmental Disorder-Not Otherwise Specified (PDD-NOS) — into a single diagnosis: autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This broadened the diagnostic criteria, resulting in more individuals falling under the ASD umbrella compared to the earlier DSM-IV framework.

At the same time, growing public awareness, evolving treatment approaches, and increased visibility of children with autism in public education settings have all contributed to higher recognition and diagnosis rates. As people become more familiar with the signs of autism, it’s more likely that individuals who may have been missed in the past are now being identified.

When looking at reported prevalence over time, earlier estimates have increased, but recent data from the CDC have shown a relatively stable pattern, hovering around 1 in 44, 1 in 36, and 1 in 31 in the last few reports. These smaller incremental changes, as opposed to sharp spikes in increases, suggest the effect of the diagnostic changes is leveling off, and we’re approaching a more accurate and consistent understanding of autism prevalence in the general population.

**What does existing research say about what causes autism?**

There’s no solid scientific evidence that points to a single cause for autism. Instead, research shows that autism is a complex condition with many different contributing factors.

These can range from genetic influences to environmental ones — or most likely, a mix of both. In fact, scientists have found links between autism and hundreds of different genes, which underscores just how multifaceted it is.

Autism isn’t something that can be “cured,” but it is best considered an alternate developmental pathway, where some are much more profoundly impaired than others. Autism is not a disease, so there is no cure. Instead, the best strategy is intervention that helps autistic individuals learn and develop skills that lead to their personal, optimal level of independence.

**Is there any research into whether environmental factors are linked to rising autism rates?**

Scientists have explored a variety of environmental toxins, none of which have been firmly implicated as a clearly linked cause that explains all — or even a significant minority — of why people have autism. There have been many changes in our environment over the past three decades that may be correlated with the rising rates of autism, from air pollution and rising carbon dioxide in our atmosphere to the use of technology and cell phones. But as we were all taught in basic high school science, correlation does not imply causation. Forgetting that basic tenet of science can lead to a significant waste of precious resources that could be better directed toward more legitimate scientific endeavors.

**What are the expected outcomes for adults with autism?**

When SARRC was founded in 1997, very little was known about the outcomes for adults with autism. The prevalence of autism was continually increasing, but long-term expectations were unclear. While many large care facilities closed in the 1980s, it was not uncommon for institutionalization to be suggested as part of the care of people with autism. Children who were diagnosed in 1997 are young adults now, and places like SARRC are working to build and shape inclusive employment and educational opportunities. According to a 2017 National Autism Indicators Report, only 14 percent of adults with autism had a job for pay outside of the home within the first two years after leaving high school. Over the next decade, it is estimated that up to 1 million youth with autism will transition to adulthood and may be seeking employment.

**What factors, if any, influence how often boys vs. girls are diagnosed with autism?**

Studies consistently find higher rates of autism in boys than girls. Currently, the male-to-female ratio for autism is estimated to be 3:1. This gender gap is narrowing (it used to be 4:1 or even slightly larger), and improvements in identifying autism in girls have led to research aiming to understand the disparity and to determine whether or not girls are being underdiagnosed. While the results are not yet definitive, the body of research that is starting to emerge is promising for early diagnosis in females, and that is invaluable. However, the gender gap is still prominent, which implicates genetics as the most likely cause of autism.

Early research on autism planted a seed for a male stereotype of the disorder and led to diagnostic procedures being largely male-biased, using male norms. In reality, females often present differently. They may have fewer repetitive behaviors, and their restricted interests may be more socially acceptable and therefore go unnoticed. They may also have a more socially appropriate communication style. With these social camouflaging traits, females are more likely to appear as if they are fitting in when they’re young, so it doesn’t raise a flag.

Common stereotypes and gendered expectations about females in general may help fuel the possibility of underdiagnosing girls. Females with autism often demonstrate some appropriate social skills. They may have good eye contact, develop language and gestures on time, and demonstrate social motivation, which can be misleading to parents and pediatricians. However, they may show subtle social differences, like making odd or too many social initiations, misreading social cues, and engaging in repetitive speech.

**How have diagnostic criteria changed in the past 20 years?**

Autistic disorder, Asperger’s disorder, and Pervasive Developmental Disorder (PDD) were three distinct developmental disorders with different diagnostic criteria, namely a lack of significant language delay in individuals with Asperger’s and an atypical onset or atypical presentation of autism associated with PDD. The division between these three developmental disorders often causes issues related to access to services as well as general care.

In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) newly identified autism as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), folding all subcategories of the condition into one umbrella diagnosis. Autistic disorder, Asperger’s disorder, and PDD are no longer considered separate conditions.

Since our founding, SARRC has remained dedicated to conducting innovative research, providing evidence-based practices, disseminating effective training, and building inclusive communities for individuals with autism and their families.

# Autism diagnoses happening earlier for boys but many girls still wait years, analysis finds

Autism diagnoses occurring earlier for boys, girls often wait years, analysis finds ABC News medical contributor Dr. Alok Patel breaks down the data from a new analysis of medical records conducted by Epic Research.

By[Dr. Christian S. Monsalve](https://abcnews.comauthor/Christian_Monsalve)

August 12, 2025, 7:20 PM

Share

Follow ABC News on Google

Autism is being diagnosed earlier in young children, especially in boys, according to a [major new analysis](https://www.epicresearch.org/articles/diagnosis-of-autism-occurring-earlier-in-children-though-still-late-for-many-initial-diagnosis-in-adulthood-increasing-in-women) of medical records published on Tuesday.

Conducted by Epic Research -- the data and analytics arm of the electronic health record software company, Epic Systems -- the analysis also found that many girls still face years-long delays in receiving a diagnosis and an increasing share of women are not diagnosed until adulthood.

This raises concerns about missed opportunities for early support, Dr. Catherine Lord, the George Tarjan Distinguished Professor of Psychiatry and Education in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, told ABC News.

[Related MORE: RFK Jr. lays out new studies on autism, shuts down 'better diagnoses' as a cause](https://abcnews.com/Health/rfk-jr-lays-new-studies-autism-shuts-diagnoses/story?id=120882735)

[](https://abcnews.com/Health/rfk-jr-lays-new-studies-autism-shuts-diagnoses/story?id=120882735)

"There is evidence that girls are often diagnosed later than boys, and particularly girls with milder symptoms are missed entirely," Lord, who was not involved in the analysis, said. "When you add in adults seeking a diagnosis later in life -- often more women than men -- it pushes the average age of diagnosis for females even higher."

The study reviewed records from more than 338,000 patients who received their first autism spectrum disorder diagnosis between 2015 and 2024, using aggregated electronic health record data from hospitals and clinics nationwide to study health care trends. While not peer-reviewed, Epic Research's work is vetted internally by the company's clinical and research experts.

![Image 3](https://i.abcnewsfe.com/a/3b2fc4b9-0875-440d-bca1-0a48cb9ba075/autism-stock-gty-jef-250812_1755023298686_hpMain.jpg)

Stock photo of a child playing with blocks.

Olena Smyrnova/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images

The median age at diagnosis for all children fell from age 7 in 2015 to age 6 in 2024, the analysis suggested. For boys, the median age dropped from age 7 to age 5, with nearly half diagnosed before age 5 in 2024.

Girls showed no similar shift, the analysis found. Their median age of diagnosis remained at about age 8, and only about one-third were diagnosed before age 5. The disparity persisted into adulthood, with one in four women first diagnosed at age 19 or older, compared with about one in eight men, the analysis found.

Although the median age for diagnosis dropped, the average age remained at about 10.5 years old, likely implying that some people were being diagnosed much later, potentially into adulthood.

Early detection matters because therapies, school accommodations, and interventions -- often involving speech-language pathologists, occupational therapists and developmental pediatricians -- are most effective when started early in life, Lord explained.

"The biggest time of change particularly in developing language, is in the early years," Lord said. "Interventions can speed up learning and help prevent later anxiety and depression by making life easier for autistic kids and their families."

[Related MORE: RFK Jr.'s comments on autism draw reactions from parents and experts](https://abcnews.com/GMA/Wellness/parents-experts-react-rfk-jrs-autism-claims/story?id=120911306)

[](https://abcnews.com/GMA/Wellness/parents-experts-react-rfk-jrs-autism-claims/story?id=120911306)

Early signs of autism can include limited eye contact, not responding to their name, delayed speech, repetitive behaviors such as hand-flapping or lining up objects, intense or unusual interests, and distress over changes in routine, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ,

In girls, these signs may be harder to notice or focused on socially typical topics, which can delay recognition.

For families facing barriers to diagnosis, Lord recommended seeking evaluations through schools, contacting state-run early intervention programs for children under age three. She also recommended relying on credible sources such as the CDC, Autism Speaks and the Autism Science Foundation for more information.

"There's much more hope now for autism," she said. "Not to 'cure' it, but to support people, figure out their strengths, and help them find their place in the world."

# Autism diagnoses happening earlier for boys but many girls still wait years, analysis finds

For boys, the median age dropped from age 7 to age 5,

![Image 2](blob:http://localhost/15fb25762162e3f215cdacd7ade0cc59)

Autism diagnoses occurring earlier for boys, girls often wait years, analysis finds ABC News medical contributor Dr. Alok Patel breaks down the data from a new analysis of medical records conducted by Epic Research.

By[Dr. Christian S. Monsalve](https://abcnews.comauthor/Christian_Monsalve)

August 12, 2025, 7:20 PM

Share

Follow ABC News on Google

Autism is being diagnosed earlier in young children, especially in boys, according to a [major new analysis](https://www.epicresearch.org/articles/diagnosis-of-autism-occurring-earlier-in-children-though-still-late-for-many-initial-diagnosis-in-adulthood-increasing-in-women) of medical records published on Tuesday.

Conducted by Epic Research -- the data and analytics arm of the electronic health record software company, Epic Systems -- the analysis also found that many girls still face years-long delays in receiving a diagnosis and an increasing share of women are not diagnosed until adulthood.

This raises concerns about missed opportunities for early support, Dr. Catherine Lord, the George Tarjan Distinguished Professor of Psychiatry and Education in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, told ABC News.

[Related MORE: RFK Jr. lays out new studies on autism, shuts down 'better diagnoses' as a cause](https://abcnews.com/Health/rfk-jr-lays-new-studies-autism-shuts-diagnoses/story?id=120882735)

[](https://abcnews.com/Health/rfk-jr-lays-new-studies-autism-shuts-diagnoses/story?id=120882735)

"There is evidence that girls are often diagnosed later than boys, and particularly girls with milder symptoms are missed entirely," Lord, who was not involved in the analysis, said. "When you add in adults seeking a diagnosis later in life -- often more women than men -- it pushes the average age of diagnosis for females even higher."

The study reviewed records from more than 338,000 patients who received their first autism spectrum disorder diagnosis between 2015 and 2024, using aggregated electronic health record data from hospitals and clinics nationwide to study health care trends. While not peer-reviewed, Epic Research's work is vetted internally by the company's clinical and research experts.

![Image 3](https://i.abcnewsfe.com/a/3b2fc4b9-0875-440d-bca1-0a48cb9ba075/autism-stock-gty-jef-250812_1755023298686_hpMain.jpg)

Stock photo of a child playing with blocks.

Olena Smyrnova/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images

The median age at diagnosis for all children fell from age 7 in 2015 to age 6 in 2024, the analysis suggested. For boys, the median age dropped from age 7 to age 5, with nearly half diagnosed before age 5 in 2024.

Girls showed no similar shift, the analysis found. Their median age of diagnosis remained at about age 8, and only about one-third were diagnosed before age 5. The disparity persisted into adulthood, with one in four women first diagnosed at age 19 or older, compared with about one in eight men, the analysis found.

Although the median age for diagnosis dropped, the average age remained at about 10.5 years old, likely implying that some people were being diagnosed much later, potentially into adulthood.

Early detection matters because therapies, school accommodations, and interventions -- often involving speech-language pathologists, occupational therapists and developmental pediatricians -- are most effective when started early in life, Lord explained.

"The biggest time of change particularly in developing language, is in the early years," Lord said. "Interventions can speed up learning and help prevent later anxiety and depression by making life easier for autistic kids and their families."

[Related MORE: RFK Jr.'s comments on autism draw reactions from parents and experts](https://abcnews.com/GMA/Wellness/parents-experts-react-rfk-jrs-autism-claims/story?id=120911306)

[](https://abcnews.com/GMA/Wellness/parents-experts-react-rfk-jrs-autism-claims/story?id=120911306)

Early signs of autism can include limited eye contact, not responding to their name, delayed speech, repetitive behaviors such as hand-flapping or lining up objects, intense or unusual interests, and distress over changes in routine, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ,

In girls, these signs may be harder to notice or focused on socially typical topics, which can delay recognition.

For families facing barriers to diagnosis, Lord recommended seeking evaluations through schools, contacting state-run early intervention programs for children under age three. She also recommended relying on credible sources such as the CDC, Autism Speaks and the Autism Science Foundation for more information.

"There's much more hope now for autism," she said. "Not to 'cure' it, but to support people, figure out their strengths, and help them find their place in the world."

About 1 in 31 US 8-year-olds (3.2%) were identified with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) 2022 surveillance year, published April 17, 2025. For **autism statistics 2026**, that is still the current figure. The CDC has not published a newer one. It replaced 1 in 36, from 2020 data published in March 2023. Every number here has its source and data year next to it.

## How common is autism in 2026? 1 in 31 children, and where that number comes from

The CDC's 1 in 31 and 1 in 36 autism figures are both correct. They describe different surveillance years. The 2022 surveillance year found 32.2 per 1,000 8-year-olds, or 1 in 31, across the 16 sites of the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network. The CDC published it in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) Surveillance Summaries 74(SS-2) on April 17, 2025.

The CDC's autism prevalence series has gone up at 9 of the 11 steps between its 12 reports since 2000. Twice it slipped: from 6.7 to 6.6 per 1,000 between the 2000 and 2002 surveillance years, and from 14.7 to 14.5 between 2010 and 2012 (CDC data table, updated May 27, 2025). Each step below carries both the year the children were counted and the date the report came out. Mixing the two up is how 1 in 36 and 1 in 31 end up in the same news story.

The CDC autism rate, one report at a time

1.   Step 1    2000

 1 in 150 8-year-olds, the first ADDM estimate  
Report and source:CDC Data and Statistics on ASD, page updated May 27, 2025 
2.   Step 2    2018

 1 in 44 (2.3%, 23.0 per 1,000)  
Report and source:[CDC MMWR 70(SS-11)](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/ss/ss7011a1.htm), published December 3, 2021 
3.   Step 3    2020

 1 in 36 (2.8%, 27.6 per 1,000) across 11 sites  
Report and source:[CDC MMWR 72(SS-2)](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/ss/ss7202a1.htm), published March 24, 2023 
4.   Step 4    2022

Report and source:CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), published April 17, 2025 
5.   Step 5   2024

 Not published as of September 5, 2026. The last 3 reports came 2 years apart (2021, 2023, 2025), so we expect it around 2027. Until then, 1 in 31 is the figure to quote through 2026  
Report and source:CDC Data and Statistics on ASD, surveillance-year table 2000 to 2022, updated May 27, 2025 

The 1 in 31 figure depends on what the CDC counted. ADDM staff review the health and special-education records of 8-year-olds in those 16 communities, home to 274,857 children that age in 2022 (they read records, they don't knock on doors) ([CDC 2025 Community Report](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/media/pdfs/2025/04/ADDM-Community-Report-SY2022.pdf), p. 13). That isn't a national sample, and the CDC says the estimate "does not necessarily represent the entire population of children in the United States" ([CDC ADDM fact sheet](https://cdc.gov/autism/communication-resources/addm-network-factsheet.html)). Where the CDC looked closely, 1 in 31 children had [autism spectrum disorder](https://prosperahealthcare.com/autism-spectrum-disorder/) documented in their records.

 Before you quote an autism figure, check 4 things 

*   - [x]    The surveillance year, not the publication year (2022 data, published 2025)    
*   - [x]    The age group (8-year-olds here, ages 3 to 17 in the parent survey, all ages in the world estimate)    
*   - [x]    The method (records review, parent survey, school eligibility count, or a model)    
*   - [x]    The coverage (16 communities, one state, or the whole country)    

Tick what you already have. This keeps count and tells you what is missing.

A figure that differs on any one of these is a different count, not a contradiction.

Source: [CDC ADDM Network fact sheet](https://cdc.gov/autism/communication-resources/addm-network-factsheet.html), 2025.

## Autism statistics in Texas: what the CDC found in its 2 Texas communities

In Laredo, one of the 2 Texas communities the CDC tracks, half of the autistic 8-year-olds had no diagnosis until 69.5 months, the latest of any ADDM site. The national median is 47 months ([CDC 2025 Community Report](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/media/pdfs/2025/04/ADDM-Community-Report-SY2022.pdf), 2022 data).

Texas joined the ADDM Network for 2022 with 2 sites. The Austin-area site, run by the University of Texas at Austin, covered part of one south-central Texas county and "did not include the city of Austin for 2022" ([CDC 2025 Community Report](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/media/pdfs/2025/04/ADDM-Community-Report-SY2022.pdf), pp. 49-50). The Laredo site covered one south Texas county, including the city of Laredo (pp. 51-52).

## Autism statistics by state: what exists instead of a 50-state ranking

The 50-state autism ranking you may have seen doesn't name its dataset. The CDC doesn't publish child prevalence for every state, and nobody has a Texas-wide child figure.

The ADDM Network's 16 communities for 2022 run from 9.7 per 1,000 in Laredo to 53.1 in California, listed in the table at the end of this section. 3 series do cover every state. None of them is a clinical count of children. Which one you want depends on who you're asking about.

## How common is autism worldwide? About 1 in 127 people

The world autism estimate went from 1 in 271 to 1 in 127 between 2 editions of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study. Autism didn't double.

The GBD 2021 study estimated 61.8 million autistic people in 2021, 1 in 127 ([Lancet Psychiatry, February 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750762/)). The World Health Organization (WHO) fact sheet, updated September 17, 2025, repeats it and notes that prevalence in many low- and middle-income countries is unknown.

The jump from GBD 2019's 1 in 271 to GBD 2021's 1 in 127 is method: GBD 2021 dropped studies that relied on passive case finding. And 1 in 127 sits below the US 1 in 31 for the same reasons: all ages against 8-year-olds, mixed methods against active record review.

## Autism in boys vs girls, and by race and ethnicity: who gets identified

Girls and children of color were once said to have less autism. In 2022 every other group was identified more often than White children, and the boy-to-girl gap was the narrowest of the last 3 reports. Both changes came from finding children who were already there.

In 2022 the CDC identified autism in 49.2 per 1,000 boys, about 1 in 20, and 14.3 per 1,000 girls, about 1 in 70. Boys were identified 3.4 times as often, down from 4.2 to 1 in 2018 and 3.8 in 2020. Among girls with autism, 40.4% had an intellectual disability, against 39.6% of all identified children: a gap under 1 point, and the CDC draws no conclusion from it. The stronger clue is the ratio itself, 4.2 to 3.4 in 4 years, which fits the CDC's explanation for rising numbers generally: more of the children who were already autistic are being identified. The [mild autism symptoms](https://prosperahealthcare.com/what-is-mild-autism/) page covers what a missed diagnosis looks like in girls.

By race and ethnicity, Asian or Pacific Islander children were identified most often in 2022 (38.2 per 1,000) and White children least (27.7). The cards below carry all 6 values (this page used to show the 2020 ones). Among children with IQ data, the share with an intellectual disability ran from 52.8% for Black children to 31.2% for multiracial children (each group's share is on its card). In some groups, only the children with the most visible needs are reaching an evaluator.

The Unbiased Science newsletter reads the reversal the same way, as better identification ([Unbiased Science, April 2025](https://theunbiasedscipod.substack.com/p/beyond-the-epidemic-headlines-what)).

## Intellectual disability, profound autism and co-occurring conditions: how often each occurs

In the CDC's 2022 data, 39.6% of autistic 8-year-olds with IQ data had an intellectual disability, and only 61.4% had ever been given an IQ test. The share is highest where testing is rarest, and the CDC says why: children are less likely to be tested "unless there is a concern" ([CDC, 2025](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/media/pdfs/2025/04/ADDM-Community-Report-SY2022.pdf)).

Intellectual disability means an IQ of 70 or below. IQ data ranged from 21.3% of cases in Laredo to 90.2% in Arkansas, and the intellectual-disability share from 24.8% in Puerto Rico to 80% in Laredo (CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), 2025). A [level of autism](https://prosperahealthcare.com/levels-of-autism/) is not an IQ score.

Profound autism means nonverbal, minimally verbal, or an IQ below 50. Hughes and colleagues applied that definition to 20,135 autistic 8-year-olds across 15 ADDM sites from 2000 to 2016 and found it fit 26.7% ([Public Health Reports, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1177/00333549231163551)). The Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC) used "approximately one-quarter" on March 17, 2026 ([HHSC](https://www.hhs.texas.gov/news/2026/03/hhsc-observes-profound-autism-awareness-day)). This page used to carry 26.7% with no source.

Co-occurring conditions are in the second set of cards below. The mental-health rates come from one analysis pooling 96 studies (Lai, Lancet Psychiatry, 2019), with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) at 28% and anxiety disorders at 20% the most common. Epilepsy runs at a median of 12.1% across studies (Lukmanji, 2019), which replaces the "up to 30%" this page used to say. ## Graduation rates and life expectancy for autistic people: which numbers hold up

The most repeated life-expectancy number for autism is probably wrong, and the researchers with the best data said so. Here it is with 2 others, each next to what its study found.

## The rising autism rate: what changed in how autism is counted

The groups rising fastest in the CDC's autism data, girls and Black and Asian children, are the ones that were undercounted before. The measuring stick got better.

How the definition and the screening of autism widened

1.   Step 1    1980

 Autism enters the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)   
2.   Step 2    1994

 DSM-IV adds Asperger syndrome   
3.   Step 3    2006

 The AAP recommends developmental screening for all children at the 9-, 18- and 30-month visits ([AAP, Pediatrics 2006](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2006-1231))   
4.   Step 4   2013

 DSM-5 folds autistic disorder, Asperger syndrome and a catch-all category into one diagnosis   

Source: [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-real-reasons-autism-rates-are-up-in-the-u-s/), 2017.

Intellectual-disability diagnoses fell as autism diagnoses rose ([Scientific American, 2017](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-real-reasons-autism-rates-are-up-in-the-u-s/)). The CDC says differences across communities "might be due to differences in availability of services for early detection and evaluation and diagnostic practices" (CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), April 2025). A true increase can't be ruled out. The data don't show one. The WHO states that research "has demonstrated that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine does not cause autism" ([WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/autism-spectrum-disorders)).

## Frequently asked questions about autism statistics

### Is it 1 in 31 or 1 in 36 children with autism?

Both 1 in 31 and 1 in 36 are CDC figures for 8-year-olds. 1 in 36 is the 2020 surveillance year, published March 2023. 1 in 31 is the 2022 surveillance year, published April 17, 2025, and it's the current number to quote for 2026.

### How many children in Texas have autism?

Nobody has a statewide clinical count of children with autism in Texas. The CDC's 2 Texas communities found autism in 1 in 51 8-year-olds (Austin-area) and 1 in 103 (Laredo) in 2022, and puts the gap down to identification rather than risk. The Texas Education Agency counts 160,218 students under the autism eligibility in 2025-26, a school category that needs no clinical diagnosis.

### Is there an autism rate for every state?

No, the CDC does not publish an autism rate for every state. The CDC's child surveillance covers 16 communities, 2 of them in Texas. For every state there's the Dietz 2020 adult model (Texas 2.19%), the NSCH parent survey for ages 3 to 17, and each state's IDEA school counts, none of which is a clinical count of children.

### Are boys really more likely to have autism?

Boys are identified with autism 3.4 times as often as girls in the CDC's 2022 data, about 1 in 20 boys against 1 in 70 girls, down from 4.2 to 1 in 2018 (CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), April 2025). The CDC counts children whose records document autism, and it attributes changes in its numbers to identification. A ratio that narrows by nearly 1 point in 4 years is consistent with girls being found who were missed before. The CDC data alone don't prove it.

### How many adults have autism?

An estimated 2.21% of US adults have autism, about 5.4 million people, and about 449,631 adults in Texas (2.19%), from a 2017 model by Dietz and colleagues published in 2020. No direct US adult autism survey exists, so the model projects child prevalence forward rather than counting adults.

### When will the CDC publish the next autism rate?

The CDC's ADDM Network has published a new autism rate for every second surveillance year since 2000 (CDC data table, updated May 27, 2025). The 2022 surveillance-year report came out on April 17, 2025, so we expect the 2024 surveillance-year report around 2027. None had been published as of September 5, 2026. Until then, 1 in 31 is the figure to quote for 2026.

Every figure on this page was checked on September 5, 2026 against the source linked next to it, a primary source wherever one exists. The figures get rechecked when the CDC publishes the 2024 surveillance-year report.

About 1 in 31 US 8-year-olds (3.2%) were identified with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) 2022 surveillance year, published April 17, 2025. For **autism statistics 2026**, that is still the current figure. The CDC has not published a newer one. It replaced 1 in 36, from 2020 data published in March 2023. Every number here has its source and data year next to it.

## How common is autism in 2026? 1 in 31 children, and where that number comes from

The CDC's 1 in 31 and 1 in 36 autism figures are both correct. They describe different surveillance years. The 2022 surveillance year found 32.2 per 1,000 8-year-olds, or 1 in 31, across the 16 sites of the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network. The CDC published it in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) Surveillance Summaries 74(SS-2) on April 17, 2025.

The CDC's autism prevalence series has gone up at 9 of the 11 steps between its 12 reports since 2000. Twice it slipped: from 6.7 to 6.6 per 1,000 between the 2000 and 2002 surveillance years, and from 14.7 to 14.5 between 2010 and 2012 (CDC data table, updated May 27, 2025). Each step below carries both the year the children were counted and the date the report came out. Mixing the two up is how 1 in 36 and 1 in 31 end up in the same news story.

The CDC autism rate, one report at a time

1.   Step 1    2000

 1 in 150 8-year-olds, the first ADDM estimate  
Report and source:CDC Data and Statistics on ASD, page updated May 27, 2025 
2.   Step 2    2018

 1 in 44 (2.3%, 23.0 per 1,000)  
Report and source:[CDC MMWR 70(SS-11)](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/ss/ss7011a1.htm), published December 3, 2021 
3.   Step 3    2020

 1 in 36 (2.8%, 27.6 per 1,000) across 11 sites  
Report and source:[CDC MMWR 72(SS-2)](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/ss/ss7202a1.htm), published March 24, 2023 
4.   Step 4    2022

 1 in 31 (3.2%, 32.2 per 1,000) across 16 sites. Of the 11 sites also in the 2020 report, 9 went up; 6.1 per 1,000 more overall  
Report and source:CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), published April 17, 2025 
5.   Step 5   2024

 Not published as of September 5, 2026. The last 3 reports came 2 years apart (2021, 2023, 2025), so we expect it around 2027. Until then, 1 in 31 is the figure to quote through 2026  
Report and source:CDC Data and Statistics on ASD, surveillance-year table 2000 to 2022, updated May 27, 2025 

The 1 in 31 figure depends on what the CDC counted. ADDM staff review the health and special-education records of 8-year-olds in those 16 communities, home to 274,857 children that age in 2022 (they read records, they don't knock on doors) ([CDC 2025 Community Report](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/media/pdfs/2025/04/ADDM-Community-Report-SY2022.pdf), p. 13). That isn't a national sample, and the CDC says the estimate "does not necessarily represent the entire population of children in the United States" ([CDC ADDM fact sheet](https://cdc.gov/autism/communication-resources/addm-network-factsheet.html)). Where the CDC looked closely, 1 in 31 children had [autism spectrum disorder](https://prosperahealthcare.com/autism-spectrum-disorder/) documented in their records.

 Before you quote an autism figure, check 4 things 

*   - [x]    The surveillance year, not the publication year (2022 data, published 2025)    
*   - [x]    The age group (8-year-olds here, ages 3 to 17 in the parent survey, all ages in the world estimate)    
*   - [x]    The method (records review, parent survey, school eligibility count, or a model)    
*   - [x]    The coverage (16 communities, one state, or the whole country)    

Tick what you already have. This keeps count and tells you what is missing.

A figure that differs on any one of these is a different count, not a contradiction.

Source: [CDC ADDM Network fact sheet](https://cdc.gov/autism/communication-resources/addm-network-factsheet.html), 2025.

## Autism statistics in Texas: what the CDC found in its 2 Texas communities

In Laredo, one of the 2 Texas communities the CDC tracks, half of the autistic 8-year-olds had no diagnosis until 69.5 months, the latest of any ADDM site. The national median is 47 months ([CDC 2025 Community Report](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/media/pdfs/2025/04/ADDM-Community-Report-SY2022.pdf), 2022 data).

Texas joined the ADDM Network for 2022 with 2 sites. The Austin-area site, run by the University of Texas at Austin, covered part of one south-central Texas county and "did not include the city of Austin for 2022" ([CDC 2025 Community Report](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/media/pdfs/2025/04/ADDM-Community-Report-SY2022.pdf), pp. 49-50). The Laredo site covered one south Texas county, including the city of Laredo (pp. 51-52).

2 state-scale autism counts for Texas have a source we could open, and neither is clinical. The Texas Education Agency (TEA) counts 160,218 students in special education under the autism eligibility in 2025-26, up from 8,650 in 2001-02 (Texas Education Research Center (ERC), UT Austin). A school eligibility isn't a diagnosis. For adults, Dietz and colleagues estimated 449,631 autistic Texans (2.19%) in 2017, a model built on child data rather than a survey.

## Autism statistics by state: what exists instead of a 50-state ranking

The 50-state autism ranking you may have seen doesn't name its dataset. The CDC doesn't publish child prevalence for every state, and nobody has a Texas-wide child figure.

The ADDM Network's 16 communities for 2022 run from 9.7 per 1,000 in Laredo to 53.1 in California, listed in the table at the end of this section. 3 series do cover every state. None of them is a clinical count of children. Which one you want depends on who you're asking about.

 Which "autism rate by state" number answers your question? 

 If you want the rate for children in Texas 

No statewide clinical count exists. The CDC's 2 Texas communities found 1 in 51 (Austin-area) and 1 in 103 (Laredo) 8-year-olds in 2022 (section above) ([CDC 2025 Community Report](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/media/pdfs/2025/04/ADDM-Community-Report-SY2022.pdf), 2022 data)

 If you want children with autism in a state's schools 

Annual counts from each state's education agency under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA): a school eligibility, not a diagnosis. Texas: 160,218 students in 2025-26 ([TEA](https://tea.texas.gov/special-populations-and-support/special-education/programs-and-services/autism), 2025-26)

 If you want adults, in Texas or any state 

The Dietz 2020 model: 2.21% of US adults, from 1.97% in Louisiana to 2.42% in Massachusetts, Texas 2.19%. Modeled from child prevalence rather than surveyed ([Dietz et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9128411/), 2017 estimates)

 If you want a parent-reported rate for children aged 3 to 17 

The National Survey of Children's Health (NSCH): 4.3% nationally in 2023-24. Its Texas estimate we haven't checked and so don't quote ([NSCH Data Resource Center](https://nschdata.org/browse/survey/results?q=11961&r=1), 2023-24)

 If you want the CDC's own child figure for a community 

The 16 ADDM sites in the table below, from 1 in 103 in Laredo to 1 in 19 in California (CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), Table 1, 2022)

 Otherwise, a ranked 50-state table that names no dataset is unsourced. 

Use one of the series above.

The NSCH survey's 4.3% (a weighted 2.66 million children aged 3 to 17, per the same NSCH table) sits above the ADDM records' 3.2% because of age (3 to 17 versus 8) and because a parent's report isn't a record review. The CDC ties California's 1 in 19 to Get SET Early, a local initiative that trained pediatricians to screen and refer early (CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), 2025).

## How common is autism worldwide? About 1 in 127 people

The world autism estimate went from 1 in 271 to 1 in 127 between 2 editions of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study. Autism didn't double.

The GBD 2021 study estimated 61.8 million autistic people in 2021, 1 in 127 ([Lancet Psychiatry, February 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11750762/)). The World Health Organization (WHO) fact sheet, updated September 17, 2025, repeats it and notes that prevalence in many low- and middle-income countries is unknown.

The jump from GBD 2019's 1 in 271 to GBD 2021's 1 in 127 is method: GBD 2021 dropped studies that relied on passive case finding. And 1 in 127 sits below the US 1 in 31 for the same reasons: all ages against 8-year-olds, mixed methods against active record review.
