## Autism in boys vs girls, and by race and ethnicity: who gets identified

Girls and children of color were once said to have less autism. In 2022 every other group was identified more often than White children, and the boy-to-girl gap was the narrowest of the last 3 reports. Both changes came from finding children who were already there.

In 2022 the CDC identified autism in 49.2 per 1,000 boys, about 1 in 20, and 14.3 per 1,000 girls, about 1 in 70. Boys were identified 3.4 times as often, down from 4.2 to 1 in 2018 and 3.8 in 2020. Among girls with autism, 40.4% had an intellectual disability, against 39.6% of all identified children: a gap under 1 point, and the CDC draws no conclusion from it. The stronger clue is the ratio itself, 4.2 to 3.4 in 4 years, which fits the CDC's explanation for rising numbers generally: more of the children who were already autistic are being identified. The [mild autism symptoms](https://prosperahealthcare.com/what-is-mild-autism/) page covers what a missed diagnosis looks like in girls.

By race and ethnicity, Asian or Pacific Islander children were identified most often in 2022 (38.2 per 1,000) and White children least (27.7). The cards below carry all 6 values (this page used to show the 2020 ones). Among children with IQ data, the share with an intellectual disability ran from 52.8% for Black children to 31.2% for multiracial children (each group's share is on its card). In some groups, only the children with the most visible needs are reaching an evaluator.

The Unbiased Science newsletter reads the reversal the same way, as better identification ([Unbiased Science, April 2025](https://theunbiasedscipod.substack.com/p/beyond-the-epidemic-headlines-what)).

## Intellectual disability, profound autism and co-occurring conditions: how often each occurs

In the CDC's 2022 data, 39.6% of autistic 8-year-olds with IQ data had an intellectual disability, and only 61.4% had ever been given an IQ test. The share is highest where testing is rarest, and the CDC says why: children are less likely to be tested "unless there is a concern" ([CDC, 2025](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/media/pdfs/2025/04/ADDM-Community-Report-SY2022.pdf)).

Intellectual disability means an IQ of 70 or below. IQ data ranged from 21.3% of cases in Laredo to 90.2% in Arkansas, and the intellectual-disability share from 24.8% in Puerto Rico to 80% in Laredo (CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), 2025). A [level of autism](https://prosperahealthcare.com/levels-of-autism/) is not an IQ score.

Profound autism means nonverbal, minimally verbal, or an IQ below 50. Hughes and colleagues applied that definition to 20,135 autistic 8-year-olds across 15 ADDM sites from 2000 to 2016 and found it fit 26.7% ([Public Health Reports, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1177/00333549231163551)). The Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC) used "approximately one-quarter" on March 17, 2026 ([HHSC](https://www.hhs.texas.gov/news/2026/03/hhsc-observes-profound-autism-awareness-day)). This page used to carry 26.7% with no source.

Co-occurring conditions are in the second set of cards below. The mental-health rates come from one analysis pooling 96 studies (Lai, Lancet Psychiatry, 2019), with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) at 28% and anxiety disorders at 20% the most common. Epilepsy runs at a median of 12.1% across studies (Lukmanji, 2019), which replaces the "up to 30%" this page used to say. Who treats these in Texas is on [mental health support for children with autism](https://prosperahealthcare.com/mental-health-services/).

## Graduation rates and life expectancy for autistic people: which numbers hold up

The most repeated life-expectancy number for autism is probably wrong, and the researchers with the best data said so. Here it is with 2 others, each next to what its study found.

| The number you'll see | What holds up | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Autistic people die 16 years earlier" | Likely incorrect, per the UK team with the best data. Their matched cohort put years of life lost at about 6 without intellectual disability (6.14 men, 6.45 women) and 7.3 (men) and 14.6 (women) with it; life expectancy of 74.6 years for men and 76.8 for women without intellectual disability, against 80.7 and 83.3 in the matched comparison group | [O'Nions et al., Lancet Regional Health Europe](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lanepe.2023.100776), November 23, 2023, open access at [PMC10769892](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10769892/) |
| "40 times higher risk of drowning death" | A share, not a risk. Among US deaths with an autism code, 1999 to 2014, 27.9% were injuries (proportionate mortality ratio, PMR, 2.93) and drowning's PMR was 39.89. A PMR compares shares of deaths: drowning made up about 40 times its usual share, which is not a 40 times higher risk of dying | [Guan and Li, American Journal of Public Health](https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2017.303696), May 2017 |
| "73.6% of autistic students graduate" | Close, but this page used to carry it with no source or year, and it matches no year we checked. In 2021-22, 72.4% of autistic students who exited school left with a regular diploma, 18.6% with an alternative certificate, and 7.0% dropped out, the lowest dropout share of any IDEA category. ## The rising autism rate: what changed in how autism is counted

The groups rising fastest in the CDC's autism data, girls and Black and Asian children, are the ones that were undercounted before. The measuring stick got better.

How the definition and the screening of autism widened

1.   Step 1    1980

 Autism enters the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)   
2.   Step 2    1994

 DSM-IV adds Asperger syndrome   
3.   Step 3    2006

 The AAP recommends developmental screening for all children at the 9-, 18- and 30-month visits ([AAP, Pediatrics 2006](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2006-1231))   
4.   Step 4   2013

 DSM-5 folds autistic disorder, Asperger syndrome and a catch-all category into one diagnosis   

Source: [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-real-reasons-autism-rates-are-up-in-the-u-s/), 2017.

Intellectual-disability diagnoses fell as autism diagnoses rose ([Scientific American, 2017](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-real-reasons-autism-rates-are-up-in-the-u-s/)). The CDC says differences across communities "might be due to differences in availability of services for early detection and evaluation and diagnostic practices" (CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), April 2025). A true increase can't be ruled out. The data don't show one. The WHO states that research "has demonstrated that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine does not cause autism" ([WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/autism-spectrum-disorders)).

## Frequently asked questions about autism statistics

### Is it 1 in 31 or 1 in 36 children with autism?

Both 1 in 31 and 1 in 36 are CDC figures for 8-year-olds. 1 in 36 is the 2020 surveillance year, published March 2023. 1 in 31 is the 2022 surveillance year, published April 17, 2025, and it's the current number to quote for 2026.

### How many children in Texas have autism?

Nobody has a statewide clinical count of children with autism in Texas. The CDC's 2 Texas communities found autism in 1 in 51 8-year-olds (Austin-area) and 1 in 103 (Laredo) in 2022, and puts the gap down to identification rather than risk. The Texas Education Agency counts 160,218 students under the autism eligibility in 2025-26, a school category that needs no clinical diagnosis.

### Is there an autism rate for every state?

No, the CDC does not publish an autism rate for every state. The CDC's child surveillance covers 16 communities, 2 of them in Texas. For every state there's the Dietz 2020 adult model (Texas 2.19%), the NSCH parent survey for ages 3 to 17, and each state's IDEA school counts, none of which is a clinical count of children.

### Are boys really more likely to have autism?

Boys are identified with autism 3.4 times as often as girls in the CDC's 2022 data, about 1 in 20 boys against 1 in 70 girls, down from 4.2 to 1 in 2018 (CDC MMWR 74(SS-2), April 2025). The CDC counts children whose records document autism, and it attributes changes in its numbers to identification. A ratio that narrows by nearly 1 point in 4 years is consistent with girls being found who were missed before. The CDC data alone don't prove it.

### How many adults have autism?

An estimated 2.21% of US adults have autism, about 5.4 million people, and about 449,631 adults in Texas (2.19%), from a 2017 model by Dietz and colleagues published in 2020. No direct US adult autism survey exists, so the model projects child prevalence forward rather than counting adults.

### When will the CDC publish the next autism rate?

The CDC's ADDM Network has published a new autism rate for every second surveillance year since 2000 (CDC data table, updated May 27, 2025). The 2022 surveillance-year report came out on April 17, 2025, so we expect the 2024 surveillance-year report around 2027. None had been published as of September 5, 2026. Until then, 1 in 31 is the figure to quote for 2026.

Every figure on this page was checked on September 5, 2026 against the source linked next to it, a primary source wherever one exists. The figures get rechecked when the CDC publishes the 2024 surveillance-year report.

AUTISM FACTS

# Top Autism Statistics in 2026

Autism Facts

Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in communication and social interaction. For the millions of individuals and families affected, understanding the scope and context of autism is an important foundation for better care, advocacy, and support.

Given recent advancements in technology, education, and behavioral science, along with the emergence of advanced clinical and data collection tools, we’re able to understand autism better and provide early intervention to aid in the development of language, learning, and social skills. Here are the most recent statistics that help support the lives of autistic individuals globally.

_These stats are backed by the CDC and other trustworthy organizations. All sources can be found at the bottom of the page._

![Image 15: Infographic showing autism prevalence statistics in kids: 1:100 worldwide, 1:31 in the US, and 3.4x in boys vs. girls.](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d2f704c775e3705253d6c9/6a6cdd1403e17564b88af40b_Autism%20stats%20in%20kids.png)

## **Key Autism Statistics**

It is estimated that **1 in every 100 children** is diagnosed with autism worldwide.

Autism affects **1 in 31 children in the US**.

Boys are diagnosed with ASD at a rate of **4 times higher than girls**.

Boys are diagnosed with ASD at a rate **3.4 times higher than girls.**

_Data sourced from the__Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)_

## Autism Rates for U.S. in 2025

**National Average:**The majority of monitored sites report an autism diagnosis prevalence between **2.5% and 3.5%**

**Highest:** California reports the highest identified autism prevalence rate at **5.3%**, followed closely by states like New Jersey and Minnesota at 3.5%

‍**Lowest:**Louisiana reports the lowest identified autism prevalence rate among all monitored sites at **1.8%** (roughly 1 in 55 children)

## Autism in Adults

**Estimated Prevalence:**Around **2.21%** of adults in the US (an estimated 5.4 million individuals aged 18 and older) are identified on the autism spectrum.

**Geographic Trends:**Adult autism prevalence percentages vary by region, ranging from a low of 1.97% in Louisiana to a high of 2.42% in Massachusetts.

**Gender Disparity:**Identified autism prevalence continues to be diagnosed at significantly higher rates in adult men than in adult women.

**Employment:**Up to 85% of autistic adults with a college education are unemployed or underemployed.

_Data sourced from the_[_CDC's Autism Spectrum Disorder in Teenagers and Adults Overview_](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/about/asd-in-teenagers-adults.html)_and the_[_Autism Society of America's Employment Statistics_](https://autismsociety.org/employment/)_._‍

## Prevalence of Autism Over Time

### Historically lower estimates

These figures likely underestimate the true prevalence due to a limited awareness of autism and narrower diagnostic criteria that excluded some individuals on the spectrum.

### Shifting landscape (1980s-2000s)

The introduction of broader diagnostic criteria in the 1980s and 1990s led to a significant rise in diagnosed cases.

Increased public awareness also contributed to higher identification of autism.

Estimates climbed to around 1 per 1,000 children in the 1980s and around 6-7 per 1,000 children by 2002 (Source: CDC).

### Continued rise and addressing under-diagnosis (2000s-present)

Recent data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) suggests a prevalence of 1 in 31 children (2025).

## Autism Rates Globally

Autism prevalence estimates vary significantly across the globe. While the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/autism-spectrum-disorders) suggests a global average of roughly 1 in 100 children, specific country data can differ substantially. Here's a breakdown of some key observations:

**Most common range:**Many countries report diagnosed autism rates between**60 and 100 per 10,000 children**. This reflects a kind of global "middle ground" in reported prevalence.

‍**Variations and influencing factors:**Important to remember, these diagnosed rates are influenced by factors like:

*   Diagnostic practices (which can differ by region).
*   Access to diagnostic services (which can vary between countries).
*   Awareness levels within a population.

**Countries with high rates:**A small number of countries report diagnosed autism rates exceeding **100 per 10,000 children**.

**Lowest reported benchmarks:**France stands out with the lowest reported diagnosed autism rate globally, with roughly 1 in 144 children identified. Again, similar considerations about influencing factors apply when interpreting this data point.

‍**Geographic distribution:**It's worth noting that countries with the lowest reported rates tend to be concentrated in Europe, while those with the highest identified rates tend to be found in East Asia and developed nations with extensive screening infrastructure. These differences reflect diagnostic systems and surveillance capacity more than any underlying biological variance across populations.

‍

_While global averages provide a baseline, advanced tracking networks reveal much higher identification rates in countries with extensive screening frameworks. For instance, the United States reports an identified prevalence that translates to roughly 320 per 10,000 children (1 in 31). This elevated rate directly reflects the implementation of comprehensive diagnostic criteria, universal pediatric screening, and high levels of public awareness regarding autism spectrum disorder._

## Autism Unemployment Rate

Autistic adults face systematic hurdles when transitioning into the workforce. The following baseline metrics highlight some of these vocational gaps.

**Low employment rates  
‍**General disability labor metrics track severe workforce exclusion, with 75% of individuals with a recognized disability remain completely outside the active labor force, according to the [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/disabl.nr0.htm).

**The college employment paradox  
‍**Higher education does not automatically mitigate traditional vocational barriers. Data highlighted by the[Autism Society of America](https://autismsociety.org/employment/) reveals that an estimated 85% of autistic adults with a college degree are unemployed or underemployed, leaving only a 15% margin fully integrated into roles that match their professional qualifications.

**Workforce integration gap  
‍  
‍**‍[Drexel University's National Autism Indicators Report](https://drexel.edu/~/media/Files/autismoutcomes/publications/Natl%20Autism%20Indicators%20Report%202017_Final.ashx) found that only about 14% of autistic adults hold paid employment in the community, a sharp gap compared with the general population.

**Difficulties beyond employment  
‍**The challenges go beyond securing employment. Obtaining social security benefits can also be difficult for autistic adults, as many haven't had the opportunity to contribute due to limited employment options.

### Potential Reasons for This Gap

**Workplace environmental obstacles  
‍**Traditional corporate environments often present intense sensory overloads, rigid social interaction dynamics, or ambiguous communication practices that can keep an autistic employee's actual professional capabilities from being recognized.

**Lack of structural accommodations  
‍**Many corporate spaces lack formalized neurodivergent support networks, structured workflows, or reasonable sensory accommodations necessary to help autistic employees thrive.

**Underutilized skill sets  
‍  
‍**General recruitment processes frequently experience an awareness deficit, focusing heavily on standard interview performance rather than recognizing the unique technical strengths, problem-solving skills, and cognitive diversity that neurodivergent professionals bring to a team.

_Data and vocational statistics compiled from the_[_U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Disability Labor Characteristics Report_](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/disabl.nr0.htm)_and the_[_Autism Society of America’s Employment Initiatives_](https://autismsociety.org/employment/)_._

_Data and vocational statistics compiled from the_[_U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Disability Labor Characteristics Report_](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/disabl.nr0.htm)_and the_[_Autism Society of America’s Employment Initiatives_](https://autismsociety.org/employment/)_._

## Percentage of Job Types for  
 Autistic People

While individuals on the autism spectrum possess a diverse and unique set of cognitive strengths, transitional research highlights specific sectors where they frequently find employment as they enter adulthood.  
  
Data from the National Longitudinal Transition Study 2 (NLTS2) indicate that office and administrative support, along with food preparation and serving, represents some of the most common vocational paths for young autistic adults in their early twenties.

#### **Key Findings and Systemic Factors**

**Closing the screening divide**: Public health indicators show that historic diagnostic barriers for minority populations are steadily being dismantled. Enhanced screening practices mean that children of color are being identified at equivalent or higher rates compared to white children within the monitored communities.

**Disparities in timely intervention:** While diagnostic _identification_ has reached statistical parity across racial lines, clinical advocates note that challenges remain regarding the age of initial evaluation and subsequent access to specialized behavioral treatments, such as Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) therapy, in underserved neighborhoods.

The data are strictly compiled from select tracking areas across 16 specific monitoring sites within the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network._

## Autism Facts

### Intellectual Disability

Based on [CDC surveillance data](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099), among autistic children with cognitive testing data, roughly 40% also have an intellectual disability. Many autistic children have average or above-average intelligence, and cognitive ability varies widely across the spectrum.

### Wandering Behavior

Nearly half [(49%) of children with autism spectrum disorder](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4983701/) between the ages of 4 and 17 are reported to have attempted to [wander or elope](https://www.motivity.net/blog/autism-elopement-risks-and-causes) from safe environments at least once. This behavior, often driven by sensory-seeking or communication difficulties, is one of the most stressful safety concerns for families.

### Autism Lifetime Costs

The [most widely cited estimate](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/1879723) puts the lifetime societal cost of supporting an individual with autism in the U.S. at about $1.4 million without an intellectual disability and $2.4 million for those with an intellectual disability. Both figures are in 2014 dollars and would be higher today in inflation-adjusted terms.

### Early Diagnosis

Behavioral symptoms of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) typically emerge early in development, often before the age of 18 months. Many children begin showing [signs of autism](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/health/topics/autism/conditioninfo/symptoms-appear#f2)[by 12 months](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/health/topics/autism/conditioninfo/symptoms-appear) or even earlier.

### Autism Risk Factors

ASD doesn't have a single cause, but multiple factors, including environmental, biological, and genetic influences, may increase the likelihood of its development. [Autism risk factors](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/about/?CDC_AAref_Val=https://www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/autism/facts.html) include having a sibling with ASD, certain genetic conditions, birth complications, and being born to older parents.

### Cognitive Functioning

Autistic individuals may have intellectual strengths in certain areas, such as mathematics, music, and art, while [facing challenges in other cognitive domains](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10916907/) like executive functioning.

### Delayed Speech Development

Children with autism spectrum disorder may experience [delays in speech and language development](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/autism-spectrum-disorder-communication-problems-children), with some not speaking at all and others developing language later in childhood.

### Sleep Disturbances

[Between 50% and 80% of children with autism experience sleep disturbances](https://www.binasss.sa.cr/bibliotecas/bhm/mar24/26.pdf), including insomnia, night waking, and poor sleep quality. These issues are often linked to sensory sensitivities, medical conditions, and behavioral challenges, significantly impacting daily functioning.

## Facts About ABA Therapy

‍

Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) is the scientific study of how the principles of behavior can be applied to create meaningful improvements in socially important skills, using systematic experimentation to identify what is actually driving those changes. ABA is used across many fields, and it is one of the most widely studied approaches for supporting autistic individuals.

_(Definition adapted from Cooper, Heron & Heward, Applied Behavior Analysis, 2nd ed., Pearson, 2007.)_

‍

### Early intensive ABA and classroom readiness

In a[2005 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16212446/) of children who received early intensive ABA (roughly 35 to 40 hours per week, modeled on the UCLA program), 48% showed rapid learning, reached average post-treatment scores, and were succeeding in regular education classrooms by age 7. Results were strongest for children who started young.

### Gains in adaptive behavior and IQ

Children who receive early intensive ABA tend to make measurable gains in IQ and adaptive behavior compared with children in standard community services. A[Cochrane review](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD009260.pub3/full) reported an average IQ gain of roughly 15 points, along with improvements in everyday living skills.

### Starting early matters

A[randomized controlled trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19948568/) of the Early Start Denver Model, an ABA-based early intervention, found that toddlers who began two years of intervention before age 3 made significantly greater gains than children referred to community services. On developmental measures, the intervention group improved by about 17.6 standard score points, compared with 7.0 points for the comparison group.

### Communication and language

Reviews of early intensive behavioral intervention report gains in expressive and receptive language and in everyday communication skills. The Early Start Denver Model trial above found consistent improvement in communication abilities as well.

### Data drive clinical decisions

Reliable data collection sits at the center of ABA, since BCBA®s rely on session data to track progress and adjust programs over time. Strong[ABA data collection methods](https://www.motivity.net/blog/aba-data-collection-methods-types-and-examples) are what make that ongoing clinical decision-making possible.

‍

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can autism be cured?

Autism is a complex neurological condition that does not have a cure. However, early therapy and intervention help individuals with autism develop communication and social skills, and enhance quality of life. Many autistic advocates and allies emphasize awareness and acceptance of differences, and promote inclusion, support, and accommodations. They also celebrate the strengths that neurodivergence can bring.

### Can autism get worse with age?

Autism doesn't get worse as you get older, but the symptoms of autism can change over time and individuals may face new challenges as they get older such as increased social isolation, difficulty accessing services, and managing co-occurring health conditions.

### Why is autism more common in males?

Autism is diagnosed more often in boys than girls, though researchers don't fully understand why. Genetic and biological differences may play a role, but a growing body of research points to diagnostic bias: autism criteria were largely developed based on how autism presents in boys, and girls are more likely to mask their traits, leading to later or missed diagnoses. The true gap may be smaller than diagnosis rates suggest.

### Can autism be detected before birth?

Autism cannot be diagnosed before birth, and there is no prenatal test for it. Some emerging research has observed possible differences in fetal development on ultrasound that may correlate with later autism, but these findings are preliminary and not used for diagnosis.

### Can autism be genetic?

Research consistently shows that autism has a genetic component and tends to run in families. Having a sibling with autism increases the likelihood of an ASD diagnosis.

# Top Autism Statistics in 2026

Autism Facts

Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in communication and social interaction. For the millions of individuals and families affected, understanding the scope and context of autism is an important foundation for better care, advocacy, and support.

Given recent advancements in technology, education, and behavioral science, along with the emergence of advanced clinical and data collection tools, we’re able to understand autism better and provide early intervention to aid in the development of language, learning, and social skills. Here are the most recent statistics that help support the lives of autistic individuals globally.

_These stats are backed by the CDC and other trustworthy organizations. All sources can be found at the bottom of the page._

![Image 15: Infographic showing autism prevalence statistics in kids: 1:100 worldwide, 1:31 in the US, and 3.4x in boys vs. girls.](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/67d2f704c775e3705253d6c9/6a6cdd1403e17564b88af40b_Autism%20stats%20in%20kids.png)

## **Key Autism Statistics**

It is estimated that **1 in every 100 children** is diagnosed with autism worldwide.

Autism affects **1 in 31 children in the US**.

Boys are diagnosed with ASD at a rate of **4 times higher than girls**.

Boys are diagnosed with ASD at a rate **3.4 times higher than girls.**

_Data sourced from the__Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)_

## Autism Rates for U.S. in 2025

**National Average:**The majority of monitored sites report an autism diagnosis prevalence between **2.5% and 3.5%**

**Highest:** California reports the highest identified autism prevalence rate at **5.3%**, followed closely by states like New Jersey and Minnesota at 3.5%

## Prevalence of Autism Over Time

### Historically lower estimates

These figures likely underestimate the true prevalence due to a limited awareness of autism and narrower diagnostic criteria that excluded some individuals on the spectrum.

### Shifting landscape (1980s-2000s)

The introduction of broader diagnostic criteria in the 1980s and 1990s led to a significant rise in diagnosed cases.

Increased public awareness also contributed to higher identification of autism.

Estimates climbed to around 1 per 1,000 children in the 1980s and around 6-7 per 1,000 children by 2002 (Source: CDC).

### Continued rise and addressing under-diagnosis (2000s-present)

Recent data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) suggests a prevalence of 1 in 31 children (2025).

## Autism Rates Globally

Autism prevalence estimates vary significantly across the globe. While the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/autism-spectrum-disorders) suggests a global average of roughly 1 in 100 children, specific country data can differ substantially. Here's a breakdown of some key observations:

**Most common range:**Many countries report diagnosed autism rates between**60 and 100 per 10,000 children**. This reflects a kind of global "middle ground" in reported prevalence.

‍**Variations and influencing factors:**Important to remember, these diagnosed rates are influenced by factors like:

*   Diagnostic practices (which can differ by region).
*   Access to diagnostic services (which can vary between countries).
*   Awareness levels within a population.

**Countries with high rates:**A small number of countries report diagnosed autism rates exceeding **100 per 10,000 children**.

**Lowest reported benchmarks:**France stands out with the lowest reported diagnosed autism rate globally, with roughly 1 in 144 children identified. Again, similar considerations about influencing factors apply when interpreting this data point.

‍**Geographic distribution:**It's worth noting that countries with the lowest reported rates tend to be concentrated in Europe, while those with the highest identified rates tend to be found in East Asia and developed nations with extensive screening infrastructure. These differences reflect diagnostic systems and surveillance capacity more than any underlying biological variance across populations.

‍

_While global averages provide a baseline, advanced tracking networks reveal much higher identification rates in countries with extensive screening frameworks. For instance, the United States reports an identified prevalence that translates to roughly 320 per 10,000 children (1 in 31). This elevated rate directly reflects the implementation of comprehensive diagnostic criteria, universal pediatric screening, and high levels of public awareness regarding autism spectrum disorder._

## Autism Unemployment Rate

Autistic adults face systematic hurdles when transitioning into the workforce. The following baseline metrics highlight some of these vocational gaps.

**Low employment rates  
‍**General disability labor metrics track severe workforce exclusion, with 75% of individuals with a recognized disability remain completely outside the active labor force, according to the [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/disabl.nr0.htm).

**The college employment paradox  
‍**Higher education does not automatically mitigate traditional vocational barriers. Data highlighted by the[Autism Society of America](https://autismsociety.org/employment/) reveals that an estimated 85% of autistic adults with a college degree are unemployed or underemployed, leaving only a 15% margin fully integrated into roles that match their professional qualifications.

**Workforce integration gap  
‍  
‍**‍[Drexel University's National Autism Indicators Report](https://drexel.edu/~/media/Files/autismoutcomes/publications/Natl%20Autism%20Indicators%20Report%202017_Final.ashx) found that only about 14% of autistic adults hold paid employment in the community, a sharp gap compared with the general population.

**Difficulties beyond employment  
‍**The challenges go beyond securing employment. Obtaining social security benefits can also be difficult for autistic adults, as many haven't had the opportunity to contribute due to limited employment options.

### Potential Reasons for This Gap

**Workplace environmental obstacles  
‍**Traditional corporate environments often present intense sensory overloads, rigid social interaction dynamics, or ambiguous communication practices that can keep an autistic employee's actual professional capabilities from being recognized.

**Lack of structural accommodations  
‍**Many corporate spaces lack formalized neurodivergent support networks, structured workflows, or reasonable sensory accommodations necessary to help autistic employees thrive.

**Underutilized skill sets  
‍  
‍**General recruitment processes frequently experience an awareness deficit, focusing heavily on standard interview performance rather than recognizing the unique technical strengths, problem-solving skills, and cognitive diversity that neurodivergent professionals bring to a team.

## Autism Facts

### Intellectual Disability

Based on [CDC surveillance data](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099), among autistic children with cognitive testing data, roughly 40% also have an intellectual disability. Many autistic children have average or above-average intelligence, and cognitive ability varies widely across the spectrum.

### Wandering Behavior

Nearly half [(49%) of children with autism spectrum disorder](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4983701/) between the ages of 4 and 17 are reported to have attempted to [wander or elope](https://www.motivity.net/blog/autism-elopement-risks-and-causes) from safe environments at least once. This behavior, often driven by sensory-seeking or communication difficulties, is one of the most stressful safety concerns for families.

### Autism Lifetime Costs

The [most widely cited estimate](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/1879723) puts the lifetime societal cost of supporting an individual with autism in the U.S. at about $1.4 million without an intellectual disability and $2.4 million for those with an intellectual disability. Both figures are in 2014 dollars and would be higher today in inflation-adjusted terms.

### Early Diagnosis

Behavioral symptoms of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) typically emerge early in development, often before the age of 18 months. Many children begin showing [signs of autism](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/health/topics/autism/conditioninfo/symptoms-appear#f2)[by 12 months](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/health/topics/autism/conditioninfo/symptoms-appear) or even earlier.

### Autism Risk Factors

ASD doesn't have a single cause, but multiple factors, including environmental, biological, and genetic influences, may increase the likelihood of its development. [Autism risk factors](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/about/?CDC_AAref_Val=https://www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/autism/facts.html) include having a sibling with ASD, certain genetic conditions, birth complications, and being born to older parents.

### Cognitive Functioning

Autistic individuals may have intellectual strengths in certain areas, such as mathematics, music, and art, while [facing challenges in other cognitive domains](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10916907/) like executive functioning.

### Delayed Speech Development

Children with autism spectrum disorder may experience [delays in speech and language development](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/autism-spectrum-disorder-communication-problems-children), with some not speaking at all and others developing language later in childhood.

### Sleep Disturbances

[Between 50% and 80% of children with autism experience sleep disturbances](https://www.binasss.sa.cr/bibliotecas/bhm/mar24/26.pdf), including insomnia, night waking, and poor sleep quality. These issues are often linked to sensory sensitivities, medical conditions, and behavioral challenges, significantly impacting daily functioning.

## Facts About ABA Therapy

‍

Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) is the scientific study of how the principles of behavior can be applied to create meaningful improvements in socially important skills, using systematic experimentation to identify what is actually driving those changes. ABA is used across many fields, and it is one of the most widely studied approaches for supporting autistic individuals.

_(Definition adapted from Cooper, Heron & Heward, Applied Behavior Analysis, 2nd ed., Pearson, 2007.)_

‍

### Early intensive ABA and classroom readiness

In a[2005 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16212446/) of children who received early intensive ABA (roughly 35 to 40 hours per week, modeled on the UCLA program), 48% showed rapid learning, reached average post-treatment scores, and were succeeding in regular education classrooms by age 7. Results were strongest for children who started young.

### Gains in adaptive behavior and IQ

Children who receive early intensive ABA tend to make measurable gains in IQ and adaptive behavior compared with children in standard community services. A[Cochrane review](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD009260.pub3/full) reported an average IQ gain of roughly 15 points, along with improvements in everyday living skills.

### Starting early matters

A[randomized controlled trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19948568/) of the Early Start Denver Model, an ABA-based early intervention, found that toddlers who began two years of intervention before age 3 made significantly greater gains than children referred to community services. On developmental measures, the intervention group improved by about 17.6 standard score points, compared with 7.0 points for the comparison group.

### Communication and language

Reviews of early intensive behavioral intervention report gains in expressive and receptive language and in everyday communication skills. The Early Start Denver Model trial above found consistent improvement in communication abilities as well.

### Data drive clinical decisions

Reliable data collection sits at the center of ABA, since BCBA®s rely on session data to track progress and adjust programs over time. Strong[ABA data collection methods](https://www.motivity.net/blog/aba-data-collection-methods-types-and-examples) are what make that ongoing clinical decision-making possible.

‍

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can autism be cured?

Autism is a complex neurological condition that does not have a cure. However, early therapy and intervention help individuals with autism develop communication and social skills, and enhance quality of life. Many autistic advocates and allies emphasize awareness and acceptance of differences, and promote inclusion, support, and accommodations. They also celebrate the strengths that neurodivergence can bring.

### Can autism get worse with age?

Autism doesn't get worse as you get older, but the symptoms of autism can change over time and individuals may face new challenges as they get older such as increased social isolation, difficulty accessing services, and managing co-occurring health conditions.

### Why is autism more common in males?

Autism is diagnosed more often in boys than girls, though researchers don't fully understand why. Genetic and biological differences may play a role, but a growing body of research points to diagnostic bias: autism criteria were largely developed based on how autism presents in boys, and girls are more likely to mask their traits, leading to later or missed diagnoses. The true gap may be smaller than diagnosis rates suggest.

### Can autism be detected before birth?

Autism cannot be diagnosed before birth, and there is no prenatal test for it. Some emerging research has observed possible differences in fetal development on ultrasound that may correlate with later autism, but these findings are preliminary and not used for diagnosis.

### Can autism be genetic?

Research consistently shows that autism has a genetic component and tends to run in families. Having a sibling with autism increases the likelihood of an ASD diagnosis.

Living with Autism | Access, Insurance & Resources

# The Best States for Autism Support

Explore the best states for autism support and how state laws impact services and resources.

![Image 3](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6627fd62e242d50407cfe155/6a2e76823f9feeabc203e479_mastermind.avif)

Mastermind Behavior Clinical Team

July 15, 2024

![Image 4: The Best States for Autism Support](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6627fd62e242d50407cfe155/6a551e9e4f74aa6afa859f4a_6a551e9c56365853099d5a61_6a3d0819ed56a6e836324919_6a3cfe74fa6ac9d9b5d8760f_states-for-autism_hero-1400.webp)

The thought you keep having, the one you have not said out loud at the dinner table yet, is whether you should move. Your child's IEP meeting did not go the way you needed it to. Every local provider has a waitlist. Someone in a Facebook group mentioned that another state has better autism services, and now you are wondering if it is true.

There is no single ranking that captures "best states for autism" cleanly. Different states lead on different things: California has the strongest entitlement framework, Massachusetts and Colorado rank high for overall family support, and [New Jersey](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/aba-therapy-in-new-jersey), [Georgia](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/aba-therapy-in-georgia), and [North Carolina](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/aba-therapy-in-north-carolina) all have strong insurance mandates that fund ABA therapy without bankrupting families. What "best" looks like for your family depends on what your child needs, what your insurance and Medicaid look like, and how close you actually live to the diagnosis, therapy, and education resources that matter day to day.

This guide walks through how to compare states on prevalence, laws, insurance, and real access.

## Understanding Autism Prevalence

Autism is a developmental disorder that affects millions of individuals worldwide. In the United States, the prevalence of autism varies widely from state to state. Understanding these variations can help inform strategies for providing services and support to individuals with autism and their families.

### State-Level Variations

The prevalence of autism among adults differs considerably across states. According to the[World Population Review](https://worldpopulationreview.com/state-rankings/autism-rates-by-state), the estimated state level prevalence of autistic adults ranges from about 1.97% in Louisiana to 2.42% in Massachusetts. South Carolina is the only other state with a prevalence below 2%, while states like New Jersey, Illinois, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, California, Connecticut, and Virginia have a high prevalence above 2.3%.

The pattern looks different for children. According to figures from the CDC's ADDM Network, California has the highest identified prevalence of autism among 8 year olds, while Texas (Laredo site) had the lowest in the most recent surveillance year. The range across ADDM sites in 2022 was 9.7 per 1,000 children at the low end to 53.1 per 1,000 at the high end[[1]](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/data-research/index.html), which is the gap that most state level "best for autism" lists are really measuring.

### Recent CDC Findings

According to the most recent CDC ADDM Network analysis, released in April 2025 with surveillance data from 2022, about 1 in 31 (3.2%) 8 year old children in the United States have been identified with autism spectrum disorder[[1]](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/data-research/index.html). That is up from the 2020 estimate of 1 in 36, which was up from 1 in 44 in 2018. The figures come from 16 communities in the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network and are not perfectly representative of the entire United States, but they are the most reliable national tracking data available.

The prevalence of ASD among children of different racial and ethnic groups has shifted significantly. In the most recent ADDM report, Asian or Pacific Islander, Black, and Hispanic children all had higher identified prevalence than White children, reversing earlier patterns and signaling improved identification in historically underserved populations.

For the first time in the ADDM record, the prevalence of autism among 8 year old girls exceeded 1%, although the male to female ratio has barely shifted from the long standing 4-to-1 pattern.

Autism prevalence in the 16 ADDM communities ranged from about 1 in 103 children in Laredo, Texas to 1 in 19 in California, highlighting variations in how communities identify children with autism. These differences offer an opportunity to compare local policies and models for delivering diagnostic and intervention services to enhance autism identification and support.

Understanding the prevalence of autism in different states and among different demographic groups is critical for planning effective support services. For more information on services and support for individuals with autism, visit our pages on[what is occupational therapy for autism?](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/what-is-occupational-therapy-for-autism) and[weighted blankets for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/weighted-blankets-for-autism).

## Factors Influencing Autism Rates

To understand the variation in identified autism rates across states, it helps to examine the factors that drive these rates. Demographic and identification patterns matter as much as the underlying biology.

### Gender Disparities

There are significant gender disparities in autism identification. Boys are roughly four times more likely to be diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder than girls. The most recent ADDM report continues to show this pattern, with overall autism prevalence about four times higher for boys than girls[[1]](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/data-research/index.html). The prevalence of autism among 8 year old girls has exceeded 1% for the first time, which still leaves a substantial diagnostic gap.

The 4-to-1 ratio has barely changed over the past decade, despite an overall rise in identified prevalence. Many researchers express skepticism that the true biological ratio is this high, suggesting that diagnostic criteria, presentation differences, and cultural expectations cause girls to be under identified[[2]](https://www.statnews.com/2023/03/23/autism-epidemic-cdc-numbers/).

Recognizing these patterns can help inform strategies to support individuals with autism and their families. The higher prevalence of identification among boys can guide the development of targeted interventions and supports, while the under identification of girls argues for more careful screening when symptoms present differently.

## Importance of State Laws

State laws play a pivotal role in shaping the landscape of support and services available to individuals with autism and their families. State law operates on top of federal law and influences the quality and availability of services at a local level.

### Impact on Support Services

State laws and policies contribute significantly to the available support and services for individuals with autism. While federal laws provide an overall framework for autism advocacy, variations in state laws and policies create real disparities in service quality and availability. Contributing factors include state level initiatives and the specific statutes and policies a given state has passed.

For instance, Alabama requires health benefit plans to provide coverage for the screening, diagnosis, and treatment of autism spectrum disorder for individuals under the age of 18. Alaska mandates certain insurers to provide coverage for the diagnosis and treatment of autism spectrum disorder for individuals under 21, effective January 1, 2013[[3]](https://www.asha.org/advocacy/state/states-specific-autism-mandates/).

### Educational Policies

Educational policies also play a significant role in supporting students with autism, promoting inclusive education, and ensuring necessary support is in place. These policies ensure students with autism have access to an education that meets their unique needs, including inclusive education practices and individualized education plans (IEPs) for appropriate support and accommodations.

For instance, Arizona requires policies issued by certain health insurers to provide coverage for the diagnosis and treatment of autism spectrum disorder, including diagnosis, assessment, and services. Behavioral therapy is specifically defined as applied behavior analysis (ABA), with coverage limits set out in the statute.

In short, the laws and regulations put in place by different states for autism can greatly affect the level and types of support services available. Families benefit from understanding these laws so they can navigate the support systems and resources available where they live.

## State Rankings for Autism Support

When it comes to providing support for individuals with autism and their families, certain states stand out for their services, resources, and policies.

### California's Leading Role

California has established a leading role in the support of individuals with autism, ranking first in grants, state laws, and ADDM inclusion. It remains the only state that has made services and supports for disabilities a true entitlement. However, due to a lack of resources in ratio to its population (massive demand, long waitlists, expensive cost of living), California does not always rank as one of the overall best states for autism support in family experience surveys.

### Supportive States Comparison

Across multi factor analyses, Colorado, Massachusetts, and New Jersey often emerge as the overall most supportive states for raising a child with autism. On the other end, West Virginia, New Mexico, and Tennessee frequently rank as the least supportive.

Several other states are also strong on autism services and support programs. For instance:

*   Georgia: Recognized for strong autism services, Georgia has implemented several autism insurance laws making it easier for families to access [early intervention and autism care](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/early-intervention-georgia).
*   Indiana: Indiana has autism insurance mandates plus organizations that provide valuable resources, education, and support to individuals and families affected by autism.
*   North Carolina: With an autism insurance mandate in place, North Carolina supports access to care without forcing families into financial hardship.
*   Oklahoma: Oklahoma has an autism insurance mandate and several organizations dedicated to improving the lives of individuals with autism and their families through education, advocacy, and support.
*   Utah: Utah offers a range of resources and organizations dedicated to autism services and support programs.

By understanding the autism support landscape across different states, families can make more informed decisions about where to seek care and resources. Whatever state you live in, resources like[occupational therapy for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/what-is-occupational-therapy-for-autism) and[weighted blankets for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/weighted-blankets-for-autism) can help with day to day symptom management.

## Legal Rights and Protections

When considering the best states for autism, it is important to understand the legal rights and protections in place for individuals with autism. These rights, anchored by federal law and reinforced by state autism laws and policies, cover equal treatment, reasonable accommodations, education, healthcare, and housing.

### Employment Accommodations

Autism should not be a barrier to gainful employment. Laws and policies require employers to provide reasonable accommodations and adjustments to support autistic individuals in the workplace. These accommodations could include assistive technologies, modified work schedules, flexible arrangements, sensory accommodations, additional training, or supports that create an inclusive work environment.

For example, an autistic adult might need certain adjustments such as a quiet workspace or use of[weighted blankets for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/weighted-blankets-for-autism) to manage sensory load. Employers can also provide additional training to help staff understand[autism and emotions](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/autism-and-emotions), fostering a more understanding workplace. Effective[transition planning](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/transition-planning) before adulthood often shapes how ready an autistic young adult is to use these workplace supports, which is why ABA therapy programs often start building vocational and self advocacy skills well before age 18.

### Healthcare and Housing

In healthcare, autistic adults have the right to access services without discrimination. This includes primary care, specialized autism services, mental health support, and other necessary medical treatments. Laws and policies require insurance coverage for autism related services, including essential interventions and therapies such as[occupational therapy for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/what-is-occupational-therapy-for-autism).

In housing, fair laws protect individuals with autism from discrimination, providing accommodations to support their unique needs and ensuring equal access to housing opportunities. Reasonable accommodations in housing might include modifications to policies, rules, or practices to create an inclusive and accessible living environment.

The legal rights and protections for individuals with autism shape the quality of life they can expect in different states. Understanding these rights helps families make informed decisions when comparing states for autism support.

## Accessing Autism Services

Beyond prevalence and legal protections, the actual day to day question for families is how easy it is to get the services your child needs. State resource disparities and insurance specifics matter more than headline rankings.

### State Resource Disparities

There is considerable variation in the availability of autism resources across different states. The average distance between an individual with autism and any of the seven resource categories (Diagnosis, Therapy, Health, Education, Recreation, Support, Other) is around 17 km nationally. However, some individuals are over 35 km away from a Diagnosis resource.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **State** | **Average Distance to Resources (km)** |
| Alaska | 100.66 |
| New Hampshire | 9.3 |

These figures highlight the need for parents and caregivers to consider the location and accessibility of resources when choosing where to live. Greater accessibility tends to translate into better outcomes for children with autism, with shorter time to diagnosis, more therapy hours actually attended, and lower family stress.

In our practice, families who relocate for autism services often find that the state's headline ranking matters less than the specific provider network within a 30 minute drive of the home address they end up at. We see this every year: a family moves to a "top ranked" state, then realizes the local BCBAs have 12 month waitlists, the plans actually available to them through their new employer cover fewer hours than they expected, and the school district is no better than the one they left. The state matters, but the radius around your home matters more.

### Insurance Coverage Considerations

Insurance coverage is another critical factor in accessing autism services. Nearly every state in the U.S. has a law requiring insurance coverage for autism treatments. However, the specifics, such as age limits and the cost categories covered for Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) therapy, can vary significantly between states. The quality of the local provider network, the credentials of the[autism behavior consultants](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/autism-behavior-consultants) and BCBAs available to you, and the in network status with your specific plan often matter more than the state mandate itself.

# The Best States for Autism Support

Explore the best states for autism support and how state laws impact services and resources.

![Image 3](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6627fd62e242d50407cfe155/6a2e76823f9feeabc203e479_mastermind.avif)

Mastermind Behavior Clinical Team

July 15, 2024

![Image 4: The Best States for Autism Support](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6627fd62e242d50407cfe155/6a551e9e4f74aa6afa859f4a_6a551e9c56365853099d5a61_6a3d0819ed56a6e836324919_6a3cfe74fa6ac9d9b5d8760f_states-for-autism_hero-1400.webp)

The thought you keep having, the one you have not said out loud at the dinner table yet, is whether you should move. Your child's IEP meeting did not go the way you needed it to. Every local provider has a waitlist. Someone in a Facebook group mentioned that another state has better autism services, and now you are wondering if it is true.

There is no single ranking that captures "best states for autism" cleanly. Different states lead on different things: California has the strongest entitlement framework, Massachusetts and Colorado rank high for overall family support, and [New Jersey](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/aba-therapy-in-new-jersey), [Georgia](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/aba-therapy-in-georgia), and [North Carolina](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/aba-therapy-in-north-carolina) all have strong insurance mandates that fund ABA therapy without bankrupting families. What "best" looks like for your family depends on what your child needs, what your insurance and Medicaid look like, and how close you actually live to the diagnosis, therapy, and education resources that matter day to day.

This guide walks through how to compare states on prevalence, laws, insurance, and real access.

## Understanding Autism Prevalence

Autism is a developmental disorder that affects millions of individuals worldwide. In the United States, the prevalence of autism varies widely from state to state. Understanding these variations can help inform strategies for providing services and support to individuals with autism and their families.

### State-Level Variations

The prevalence of autism among adults differs considerably across states. According to the[World Population Review](https://worldpopulationreview.com/state-rankings/autism-rates-by-state), the estimated state level prevalence of autistic adults ranges from about 1.97% in Louisiana to 2.42% in Massachusetts. South Carolina is the only other state with a prevalence below 2%, while states like New Jersey, Illinois, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, California, Connecticut, and Virginia have a high prevalence above 2.3%.

The pattern looks different for children. According to figures from the CDC's ADDM Network, California has the highest identified prevalence of autism among 8 year olds, while Texas (Laredo site) had the lowest in the most recent surveillance year. The range across ADDM sites in 2022 was 9.7 per 1,000 children at the low end to 53.1 per 1,000 at the high end[[1]](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/data-research/index.html), which is the gap that most state level "best for autism" lists are really measuring.

### Recent CDC Findings

According to the most recent CDC ADDM Network analysis, released in April 2025 with surveillance data from 2022, about 1 in 31 (3.2%) 8 year old children in the United States have been identified with autism spectrum disorder[[1]](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/data-research/index.html). That is up from the 2020 estimate of 1 in 36, which was up from 1 in 44 in 2018. The figures come from 16 communities in the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network and are not perfectly representative of the entire United States, but they are the most reliable national tracking data available.

The prevalence of ASD among children of different racial and ethnic groups has shifted significantly. In the most recent ADDM report, Asian or Pacific Islander, Black, and Hispanic children all had higher identified prevalence than White children, reversing earlier patterns and signaling improved identification in historically underserved populations.

For the first time in the ADDM record, the prevalence of autism among 8 year old girls exceeded 1%, although the male to female ratio has barely shifted from the long standing 4-to-1 pattern.

Autism prevalence in the 16 ADDM communities ranged from about 1 in 103 children in Laredo, Texas to 1 in 19 in California, highlighting variations in how communities identify children with autism. These differences offer an opportunity to compare local policies and models for delivering diagnostic and intervention services to enhance autism identification and support.

Understanding the prevalence of autism in different states and among different demographic groups is critical for planning effective support services. For more information on services and support for individuals with autism, visit our pages on[what is occupational therapy for autism?](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/what-is-occupational-therapy-for-autism) and[weighted blankets for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/weighted-blankets-for-autism).

## Factors Influencing Autism Rates

To understand the variation in identified autism rates across states, it helps to examine the factors that drive these rates. Demographic and identification patterns matter as much as the underlying biology.

### Gender Disparities

There are significant gender disparities in autism identification. Boys are roughly four times more likely to be diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder than girls. The most recent ADDM report continues to show this pattern, with overall autism prevalence about four times higher for boys than girls[[1]](https://www.cdc.gov/autism/data-research/index.html). The prevalence of autism among 8 year old girls has exceeded 1% for the first time, which still leaves a substantial diagnostic gap.

The 4-to-1 ratio has barely changed over the past decade, despite an overall rise in identified prevalence. Many researchers express skepticism that the true biological ratio is this high, suggesting that diagnostic criteria, presentation differences, and cultural expectations cause girls to be under identified[[2]](https://www.statnews.com/2023/03/23/autism-epidemic-cdc-numbers/).

Recognizing these patterns can help inform strategies to support individuals with autism and their families. The higher prevalence of identification among boys can guide the development of targeted interventions and supports, while the under identification of girls argues for more careful screening when symptoms present differently.

## Importance of State Laws

State laws play a pivotal role in shaping the landscape of support and services available to individuals with autism and their families. State law operates on top of federal law and influences the quality and availability of services at a local level.

### Impact on Support Services

State laws and policies contribute significantly to the available support and services for individuals with autism. While federal laws provide an overall framework for autism advocacy, variations in state laws and policies create real disparities in service quality and availability. Contributing factors include state level initiatives and the specific statutes and policies a given state has passed.

For instance, Alabama requires health benefit plans to provide coverage for the screening, diagnosis, and treatment of autism spectrum disorder for individuals under the age of 18. Alaska mandates certain insurers to provide coverage for the diagnosis and treatment of autism spectrum disorder for individuals under 21, effective January 1, 2013[[3]](https://www.asha.org/advocacy/state/states-specific-autism-mandates/).

### Educational Policies

Educational policies also play a significant role in supporting students with autism, promoting inclusive education, and ensuring necessary support is in place. These policies ensure students with autism have access to an education that meets their unique needs, including inclusive education practices and individualized education plans (IEPs) for appropriate support and accommodations.

For instance, Arizona requires policies issued by certain health insurers to provide coverage for the diagnosis and treatment of autism spectrum disorder, including diagnosis, assessment, and services. Behavioral therapy is specifically defined as applied behavior analysis (ABA), with coverage limits set out in the statute.

In short, the laws and regulations put in place by different states for autism can greatly affect the level and types of support services available. Families benefit from understanding these laws so they can navigate the support systems and resources available where they live.

## State Rankings for Autism Support

When it comes to providing support for individuals with autism and their families, certain states stand out for their services, resources, and policies.

### California's Leading Role

California has established a leading role in the support of individuals with autism, ranking first in grants, state laws, and ADDM inclusion. It remains the only state that has made services and supports for disabilities a true entitlement. However, due to a lack of resources in ratio to its population (massive demand, long waitlists, expensive cost of living), California does not always rank as one of the overall best states for autism support in family experience surveys.

### Supportive States Comparison

Across multi factor analyses, Colorado, Massachusetts, and New Jersey often emerge as the overall most supportive states for raising a child with autism. On the other end, West Virginia, New Mexico, and Tennessee frequently rank as the least supportive.

Several other states are also strong on autism services and support programs. For instance:

*   Georgia: Recognized for strong autism services, Georgia has implemented several autism insurance laws making it easier for families to access [early intervention and autism care](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/early-intervention-georgia).
*   Indiana: Indiana has autism insurance mandates plus organizations that provide valuable resources, education, and support to individuals and families affected by autism.
*   North Carolina: With an autism insurance mandate in place, North Carolina supports access to care without forcing families into financial hardship.
*   Oklahoma: Oklahoma has an autism insurance mandate and several organizations dedicated to improving the lives of individuals with autism and their families through education, advocacy, and support.
*   Utah: Utah offers a range of resources and organizations dedicated to autism services and support programs.

By understanding the autism support landscape across different states, families can make more informed decisions about where to seek care and resources. Whatever state you live in, resources like[occupational therapy for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/what-is-occupational-therapy-for-autism) and[weighted blankets for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/weighted-blankets-for-autism) can help with day to day symptom management.

## Legal Rights and Protections

When considering the best states for autism, it is important to understand the legal rights and protections in place for individuals with autism. These rights, anchored by federal law and reinforced by state autism laws and policies, cover equal treatment, reasonable accommodations, education, healthcare, and housing.

### Employment Accommodations

Autism should not be a barrier to gainful employment. Laws and policies require employers to provide reasonable accommodations and adjustments to support autistic individuals in the workplace. These accommodations could include assistive technologies, modified work schedules, flexible arrangements, sensory accommodations, additional training, or supports that create an inclusive work environment.

For example, an autistic adult might need certain adjustments such as a quiet workspace or use of[weighted blankets for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/weighted-blankets-for-autism) to manage sensory load. Employers can also provide additional training to help staff understand[autism and emotions](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/autism-and-emotions), fostering a more understanding workplace. Effective[transition planning](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/transition-planning) before adulthood often shapes how ready an autistic young adult is to use these workplace supports, which is why ABA therapy programs often start building vocational and self advocacy skills well before age 18.

### Healthcare and Housing

In healthcare, autistic adults have the right to access services without discrimination. This includes primary care, specialized autism services, mental health support, and other necessary medical treatments. Laws and policies require insurance coverage for autism related services, including essential interventions and therapies such as[occupational therapy for autism](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/what-is-occupational-therapy-for-autism).

In housing, fair laws protect individuals with autism from discrimination, providing accommodations to support their unique needs and ensuring equal access to housing opportunities. Reasonable accommodations in housing might include modifications to policies, rules, or practices to create an inclusive and accessible living environment.

The legal rights and protections for individuals with autism shape the quality of life they can expect in different states. Understanding these rights helps families make informed decisions when comparing states for autism support.

## Accessing Autism Services

Beyond prevalence and legal protections, the actual day to day question for families is how easy it is to get the services your child needs. State resource disparities and insurance specifics matter more than headline rankings.

### State Resource Disparities

There is considerable variation in the availability of autism resources across different states. The average distance between an individual with autism and any of the seven resource categories (Diagnosis, Therapy, Health, Education, Recreation, Support, Other) is around 17 km nationally. However, some individuals are over 35 km away from a Diagnosis resource.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **State** | **Average Distance to Resources (km)** |
| Alaska | 100.66 |
| New Hampshire | 9.3 |

These figures highlight the need for parents and caregivers to consider the location and accessibility of resources when choosing where to live. Greater accessibility tends to translate into better outcomes for children with autism, with shorter time to diagnosis, more therapy hours actually attended, and lower family stress.

In our practice, families who relocate for autism services often find that the state's headline ranking matters less than the specific provider network within a 30 minute drive of the home address they end up at. We see this every year: a family moves to a "top ranked" state, then realizes the local BCBAs have 12 month waitlists, the plans actually available to them through their new employer cover fewer hours than they expected, and the school district is no better than the one they left. The state matters, but the radius around your home matters more.

### Insurance Coverage Considerations

Insurance coverage is another critical factor in accessing autism services. Nearly every state in the U.S. has a law requiring insurance coverage for autism treatments. However, the specifics, such as age limits and the cost categories covered for Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) therapy, can vary significantly between states. The quality of the local provider network, the credentials of the[autism behavior consultants](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/autism-behavior-consultants) and BCBAs available to you, and the in network status with your specific plan often matter more than the state mandate itself.

| Arizona | Required for diagnosis, assessment, and services, including applied behavioral analysis. |

Treatment includes Applied Behavior Analysis, pharmacy care, psychiatric care, psychological care, therapeutic care provided by licensed speech therapists, occupational therapists, or physical therapists, and necessary equipment for evidence-based treatment determined by a licensed physician. |
| California | Required for all health care service plan contracts to provide coverage for behavioral health treatment for pervasive developmental disorder or autism no later than July 1, 2012. Treatments include professional services and treatment programs, including applied behavior analysis, speech-language pathology, and audiology. |

Details courtesy[ASHA](https://www.asha.org/advocacy/state/states-specific-autism-mandates/).
