## Abstract

Autism diagnosis before age three to speed access to critical services is a public health priority in the United States. Still, the average age of autism diagnosis is 49 months with substantial variability across states. By examining policy – defined as laws, regulations, procedures, administrative actions, incentives, or voluntary practices of governments or other institutions – modifiable structural drivers of early (or late) autism diagnosis may be identified. We, therefore, sought to identify policies impacting early autism diagnosis in five states that are part of a larger initiative to improve autism diagnosis (Arizona, California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania) and those that exist nationally. We conducted semi-structured interviews from 2021 to 2023 with a purposive sample of 57 autism policy or research experts. The following four themes were identified through conventional content analysis: (1) developmental monitoring is critical; however, developmental screening policies vary within and across states; (2) myriad policy and contextual factors shape early diagnosis pathways within states; (3) state early intervention and community-based early childhood programs influence early autism diagnosis; and (4) persistent disparities in early autism diagnosis pathways are affected by policy. Study findings highlight the importance of advancing certain state and federal policies to increase early autism diagnosis.

## Abstract

In the United States, when children on the spectrum are diagnosed before age three it can help them get the services they need to thrive. There are many differences between states as far as how many children are diagnosed with autism and the average age when they are diagnosed. Some work suggests these differences may be due to state polices, which include the laws and processes governments and organizations follow. Little research has tried to understand the similarities and differences between state policies related to autism diagnosis. Because of this, our study looked at how state policies impact the timing of autism diagnosis in the United States. We interviewed 57 experts in five states and nationally from 2021–2023. Four key themes were identified including (1) developmental monitoring often leads to screening but there is much variation in and across states; (2) family, community, and healthcare factors shape pathways to autism diagnosis in states; (3) early intervention and education programs play a role in autism diagnosis; and (4) systematic differences in access to diagnosis services persist for certain groups of children and families such as those with limited English speaking abilities. This study’s findings point to certain state and federal policy changes or enhancements to reduce the age of autism diagnosis and ameliorate persistent disparities in autism diagnosis.

**Keywords:**autism, disparities, insurance, early diagnosis, policy, services, United States

## Method

### Design and data availability

This qualitative investigation was embedded in a larger multisite randomized controlled trial (RCT) on the outcomes of a family navigation model on early autism diagnosis, which originally involved three sites that were part of the Developmental-Behavioral Pediatrics Research Network in Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania (Blum & the DBPNet Steering Committee, 2012; Broder-Fingert et al., 2018; Feinberg et al., 2021, 2023). Two west coast sites in Arizona and California were added based on the past research of study collaborators and to increase geographic diversity. Given limited relevant topical evidence, we used a grounded theory approach with in-depth, semi-structured interviews (Glaser & Strauss, 1999; Jacobsen, 2021). The larger study’s institutional review board approved this qualitative investigation. Because the data gathered for this study are potentially identifiable and the informed consent process did not include obtaining participant permission for public data sharing, the data may be requested by contacting the authors.

### Sampling and recruitment

Purposive criterion and snowball sampling (Palinkas et al., 2015) were used to recruit individuals from the five states (Arizona, California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania) where the larger study was conducted. Based on a literature review and the study team members’ expertise, we identified individuals who had worked on and/or conducted research about autism policy to interview and invited them to participate. Participants were asked to provide contact information for any colleague(s) who could possibly contribute to the study, given their work and/or research experience related to autism policy. The same sampling strategy was used to recruit national autism policy experts, who had worked on and/or conducted research about autism policy across states. Fifty-six interviews were conducted with 57 participants (one interview was with two participants).

### Participant characteristics

As shown in Table 1, the participants’ average age was 49 years, and 82.5% were female. Participants represented a variety of professional backgrounds including researchers from academic institutions, clinical psychologists, medical providers (i.e., general pediatricians, Developmental Behavioral Pediatricians), advocates, professionals from local- or state-level government agencies, professionals from the health insurance sector, and professionals from the Individuals with Disabilities Part C Early Intervention (EI) system. Participants represented 10 states: Arizona, California, Connecticut, Indiana, Massachusetts, Missouri, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, and Utah.

### Data collection

From 2021 to 2023, five qualitatively trained research team members conducted interviews with participants via Zoom due to the ongoing impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and the geographic dispersion of participants’ locations. Participants provided verbal consent; interviews lasted 45 to 60 minutes. Data collection in each of the five states continued until the researchers had conducted more than five interviews or the research team concluded that data saturation was reached (Guest et al., 2016). Interviews were audio recorded and transcribed verbatim; transcripts were de-identified.

### Interview guide

The interview guide was informed by literature on early autism diagnosis (Lindly et al., 2024), a review of policy databases (i.e., LexisNexis), and the qualitative arm of a prior RCT on Family Navigation (Broder-Fingert et al., 2018). The guide included unstructured questions and directed probes addressing topics on the typical autism diagnostic pathway within the participant’s state of residence, state policies promoting early autism diagnosis and other services use, the influence of disparities on the accessibility of early autism diagnosis, and suggestions for improving early autism diagnosis in the state. Interviews conducted with national autism experts examined these topics in terms of national initiatives and the influence of variability across multiple states. The in-depth interview guide including guiding questions and probes are provided in the supplemental material.

### Analysis

A conventional content analysis was used in NVivo. Conventional content analysis is aligned with a grounded theory approach to qualitative research because it is intended to help describe a phenomenon for which there is little theoretical underpinning and existing evidence (Glaser & Strauss, 1999; Hsieh & Shannon, 2005). A coding scheme was collaboratively developed by three research team members based on the interview guide and from an independent review of six interview transcripts. Elemental coding methods were used including descriptive, in vivo, and structural coding (Saldaña, 2021). Sample structural codes included “Autism Screening Policy Factors,” “Disparities in Early Diagnosis,” and “State Early Diagnosis Policy Factors.” Sample subcodes included “Local or Regional Autism Screening Policy Factors,” “Racial or Ethnic Disparities in Early Diagnosis,” and “State Laws Impacting Early Diagnosis.”

Coding began in 2022, while the interviews were still being conducted, with three research team members meeting weekly to discuss questions related to their coding and resolve inconsistencies in coding through consensus. The coding scheme underwent iterative revision until two research team members had independently coded each transcript. Coding consistency was assessed for each code by having one research team member review all coding by two other research team members and propose changes to coding and the scheme to the larger coding team. We identified themes, subthemes and exemplar quotations by collectively examining the coding within and across codes and their respective subcodes. Themes and subthemes were additionally mapped by three research team members to relevant policy recommendations made by the interview participants.

### Member-checking

To establish thematic validity and ensure the utility of study findings for autistic community members, we engaged a subset of five interview participants who identified as parents of autistic children or as an autistic individual in member checking, some also had relevant professional expertise such as clinical psychologist or psychiatrist (characteristics indicated in Table 1). We adapted the meaningful member-checking process and questions (McKim, 2023) to incorporate participants’ perspectives in engaging, adding to, and aiding in the interpretation of interview data (Birt et al., 2016). We asked each member-checking participant to review a list of draft themes, subthemes, and policy recommendations along with exemplar quotes prior to engaging in a one to two hour long virtual interview with them about their thoughts on the list. Member-checking findings were used to revise the draft themes, subthemes, and policy recommendations; these revisions included adding information and integrating contradictory perspectives.

### Community involvement and authors’ positionality

We involved community members in this study by interviewing parents of autistic children and autistic adults. We additionally conducted member checking of the themes distilled from the interview data with a subset of these community members who were originally interviewed. The interdisciplinary research team that conducted this study possesses expertise in pediatrics, public health including health policy and services research, and psychology. Three research team members are also practicing clinicians. An autistic researcher on the study team participated in data collection and analysis, drafting, and critical revision of the manuscript. The other authors identify themselves as neurotypical academic researchers. Our ongoing research collaborations, clinical practice, and lived experiences as parents and family members also shaped this study.

## Results

Major themes and subthemes related to cross-cutting policy and contextual factors within and between states affecting early autism diagnosis are presented. Exemplary quotations are provided to help illustrate key findings. Member-checking perspectives are integrated throughout each subsection. Two summary tables with exemplar quotations including one table with the major themes and subthemes and one table with the policy recommendations are provided (Tables 2 and 3). Policy recommendation findings are integrated in the Discussion.

### Themes and Subthemes on State Policy and Contextual Factors Affecting Early Autism Diagnosis

The following four overarching themes emerged: (1) developmental monitoring is critical; however, developmental screening procedures, actions, and practices vary within and across states; (2) myriad policy and contextual factors at the family, provider, community, and health system levels shape early diagnosis pathways within states; (3) state EI and community-based early childhood program regulations, procedures, and practices influence early autism diagnosis; and (4) persistent disparities in early autism diagnosis pathways are affected by regulations, procedures, actions, and practices. Subthemes were identified, and member-checking findings were integrated for each theme.

#### Theme 1.

Developmental monitoring is critical; however, developmental screening procedures, actions, and practices vary within and across states. Developmental monitoring often precedes autism assessment per national guidelines (Lipkin et al., 2020). Routine ages are designated for developmental and autism-specific screening in young children. Yet variability in policies within and across states was reported to affect screening periodicity and the instrumentation used.

##### Subtheme 1a. Variable implementation of development monitoring initiatives exists.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and other organizations have launched initiatives such as Learn the Signs. Act Early. which are designed to provide educational materials on children’s developmental milestones within the first five years of life (Daniel et al., 2009). The Act Early component of the CDC program includes Act Early ambassadors who are professionals assigned to integrate this work into their state’s efforts to improve early identification (e.g., disseminating Milestone Moments booklets at early care centers, offering statewide training in autism case identification; National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2023). Despite being partnered with national, regional, and local organizations, some participants reported that the ambassadors’ work may not have a broad, equitable reach for families within their states. This may be due to collaborations being formed voluntarily, and ambassadors not covering all areas within states (e.g., sovereign tribal nations).

##### Subtheme 1b. Lack of state/federal developmental screening/monitoring mandate.

Although the AAP recommends that pediatric PCPs conduct autism-specific screening when children turn 18-months old, some participants noted that this guideline has not been codified in state or federal policies. Participants further described how this lack of screening policy may contribute to inconsistent screening practices, such as providers not conducting screening at all recommended ages, only administering autism-specific screeners like the M-CHAT when children demonstrate heightened autism symptomatology or not administering the M-CHAT’s follow-up interview. One participant elaborated as follows:

> I ended up contacting all of the practices that were involved in this […] healthcare system-wide study where I was able to administratively look at the proportion of 18-to-24-month old’s that received autism screening. And, then I was able to look in their medical records to see who had an autism diagnosis later on. And I contacted all these practices, and I asked their providers directly, like, can you just tell me about the usual process of autism screening? And, what we found is that the vast majority had either never heard of the second step [follow-up interview] of the M-CHAT or had significant issues in terms of how it was administered. It’s a 15 to 20-minute interview. [I]t doesn’t fit into clinical practice easily.”
> 
> 
> (Participant 47, Utah)

##### Subtheme 1c. Context-specific use of developmental screening tools.

Some participants expressed that while primary care practices may use autism-specific screeners such as the M-CHAT, EI or Head Start programs’ developmental screening can be limited to broad developmental screeners (e.g., ASQ). The use of more general development screeners was attributed to the focus on developmental conditions more broadly. Member checking findings supported the use of different screeners in different contexts because of the type of information most useful to specific contexts. For example, for early childhood education programs, the information yielded from broad developmental screeners may be more helpful to holistically understanding the child’s development.

#### Theme 2.

Myriad policy and contextual factors at the family, provider, community, and health system levels shape early diagnosis pathways within states. Autism assessment pathways often include multiple steps such as screening, referral, evaluation, and diagnosis. Many participants expressed how numerous factors contribute to the variability in autism assessment pathways within and across states. Moreover, participants described how the factors affecting autism assessment pathways are often at various levels of influence including the family level (e.g., parent’s autism-related health literacy), the provider level (e.g., provider’s ability to identify autism risk and complete diagnostic testing), the community level (e.g., availability of autism diagnosticians in certain geographic areas), and the health system level (e.g., public health insurance reimbursement rates for autism assessment). Five related subthemes were identified.

##### Subtheme 2a. Multiple referral sources for autism diagnostic evaluation.

Participants discussed the lack of uniform referral for autism diagnosis in the United States. Some participants noted how young children are often referred by their PCP for autism evaluation after screening positive for elevated autism likelihood on the M-CHAT at a well-child visit. Participants additionally described how some PCPs will refer children for autism evaluation after scoring their M-CHAT, while other providers may request that the child’s parent(s) seek out the autism evaluation. As one participant explained: “I would say that mostly I hear about families having completed the M-CHAT, but typically what happens is that a provider, like a pediatrician, would say that they were worried, and it might be because of an M-CHAT score, and then the family would call us directly, so I think that’s the majority. Like sometimes the provider gives them our name, but usually, it’s the family that’s coming through our door.”(Participant 13, California) Although participants mentioned how little developmental screening in EI programs is autism-specific, they also noted that in some states, EI programs do refer children for autism diagnostic evaluations. Several participants noted that their state’s EI program can directly provide autism evaluations if diagnosticians are part of the program. Another path to diagnosis and services that they described was a category of children who receive a medical diagnosis of autism before enrolling in EI services. Member-checking findings supported the notion of multiple referral sources and paths to autism diagnosis, which may impact timeliness of access to diagnosis and services.

##### Subtheme 2b. Lengthy wait times and provider shortages.

Many participants described the lengthy wait times that families commonly experience throughout their child’s diagnostic odyssey. Participants articulated that one of the driving forces behind this phenomenon is shortages in qualified diagnosticians, which prevents clinics from sufficiently meeting the demand for autism evaluation. The amount of time that a family spends on a waitlist for an autism evaluation was further described as being dependent upon the child’s age insofar as certain clinics prioritize scheduling evaluations for children who are younger than three years old to ensure that these children can be referred for therapy services promptly. Whereas the families of children who are referred for diagnostic evaluations at older ages often find themselves on the waitlist for longer periods, which may also delay their access to therapy services.

> “…[I]n order to try to prioritize younger children to help them get that diagnosis as early as possible. We have adjusted the way our wait-list system works so that children under three can come in and they’re prioritized for quick visits and children who get referred to us after age three are placed on a wait list. So, unfortunately, that really delays the assessments for children who are over three, but the trade-off is that then we can try to get more children in at a younger age, if they come before three.”
> 
> 
> (Participant 3, Pennsylvania)

##### Subtheme 2c. Required usage of specific diagnostic instruments.

Autism diagnostic assessments, such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule Second Edition (ADOS-2), were recognized by some participants as “gold standard” diagnostic tools. The ADOS and other commonly used assessments (e.g., the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised) are not, however, required for providers to make a medical autism diagnosis. Participants described an increased reliance on these tools to diagnose autism as being driven by requirements for coverage of autism-related services. For example, many insurance companies and Medicaid require that certain assessment tools be used to determine an autism diagnosis in order to cover certain autism services (e.g., ABA therapy). The use of these ‘gold-standard’ autism assessments was also noted as impeding diagnosis in part due to the extensive provider training needed to use these tools. Member-checking findings highlighted the view that a variety of autism assessment tools should be permitted in making an autism diagnosis and that insurance companies should not act as gatekeepers for services based on what assessment tool is used. One participant further expressed that parent interview components of diagnostic tools should be valued more than play-based or observation-based assessment activities. Another participant described how the training standards for autism assessment use are helpful in ensuring diagnostic reliability and accuracy.

##### Subtheme 2d. Medicaid coverage barriers.

Many participants noted that children with Medicaid often have a more challenging time obtaining autism evaluation due to low reimbursement rates and limited providers who will accept Medicaid coverage for autism evaluation across the five states. These challenges with Medicaid coverage and access to autism diagnostic services were attributed to longer wait times for poor and rural families, thereby perpetuating inequity in early autism diagnosis. According to one participant: “We have […] approximately 50, that I know of, professionals that can diagnose autism. Or actively do. Out of that 50, there’s probably five, that I know, who are quality, qualified autism experts that accept AHCCCS [Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System, Medicaid] payments for those evaluations. So, if you don’t have private insurance or you can’t afford a private evaluation, you are…sent to Phoenix Children’s Hospital. And their wait list is…12 to 18 months.”(Participant 33, Arizona) Participants additionally explained that when an autism evaluation does not yield a diagnosis, parents may be forced to pay out of pocket for the evaluation because their insurance plan will not cover the cost. Nevertheless, participants explained how some healthcare organizations have determined ways to ensure that children with Medicaid receive an autism diagnosis. For example, several participants described that some academic medical centers could pursue supplemental payment for low Medicaid reimbursement rates through state programs such as early and periodic screening, diagnostic, and treatment (EPSDT). Some participants elaborated that Medicaid coverage may be a greater barrier to early diagnosis in states where the Medicaid program does not accept autism as a qualifying diagnosis (regardless of income) for eligibility.

##### Subtheme 2e. State requirements on autism diagnosis as a hindrance to early diagnosis.

Participants in certain states, such as Arizona, described that insurance plans and state agencies that provide services for individuals with developmental disabilities will only authorize coverage for autism-related therapy services if the child received an autism diagnosis from select types of medical providers (e.g., DBP, neurologist, clinical psychologist, psychiatrist). Participants from all five states reported their state has imposed regulations impacting the acceptability of autism diagnoses. Participants described these regulations as a driving factor in lengthy wait times for autism evaluation and delayed diagnosis given the workforce shortages in each of these specialties. “The state policy that only an MD/DO can make the diagnosis or has a PhD, has severely impacted the ability to give the diagnosis before the age of three because it’s vastly decreased the number of clinicians who are qualified to make that diagnosis[…] there are not enough MDs/DOs, PhDs who feel confident and are qualified to make the diagnosis […].”(Participant 27, Massachusetts) Member checking findings confirmed the view that current regulations around which provider types are authorized to diagnose autism are too restrictive. Participants acknowledged that expanding provider types to include some PCPs such as general pediatricians could be beneficial to reducing diagnostic wait times and increasing early autism diagnosis. Still, some participants cautioned against including certain primary care provider types that may not be required to have training in pediatrics and autism more specifically.

#### Theme 3.

State EI and community-based early childhood program regulations, procedures, and practices influence early autism diagnosis. Since EI may be a referral source for autism evaluation and in some cases, a place where children are diagnosed, both EI and other early childhood were recognized as contributing to early diagnosis. Two subthemes further emerged.

##### Subtheme 3a. Usage of provisional “at-risk” for autism diagnoses by state EI programs.

Due to lengthy wait times for autism evaluation and the need for children to begin therapy services as young as possible to maximize possible benefits, participants described how state EI programs may provide children with provisional “at-risk” autism diagnoses. Participants in some states further noted that provisional diagnoses allow children in Early Intervention (EI) who are at risk for autism to access autism-specific therapy services. One participant explained how this may unfold for children in California: “So, we have regional centers in California and regional centers, they vary a lot. [..]. So, if a child shows delays, even if formal diagnostic criteria for autism aren’t met or if the regional center isn’t ready to make […] so they don’t really make diagnoses, but they’ll determine whether somebody is eligible to be a client of regional center and an autism diagnosis would definitely […] qualify you for the long term.”(Participant 13, California) While EI services are no longer available after age 3, children with a provisional autism diagnosis will have been evaluated by professionals while awaiting a medical diagnosis. Participants including those who underwent member-checking interviews, expressed that a provisional diagnosis is often not equivalent to a medical diagnosis. That is, many state disability programs require children to receive a medical autism diagnosis before enrolling in autism-specific therapy services. Member-checking findings supported that provisional autism diagnoses can have positive impacts by enabling children to access helpful therapy services from a younger age. One participant further noted how autism diagnoses are important to ensuring that children receive beneficial services as young as possible. Some participants cautioned that EI providers may not have adequate training to make autism diagnoses including provisional diagnoses.

##### Subtheme 3b. The timing of autism diagnosis influences access to treatment services.

Participants described that many families who have developmental concerns about their child will pursue an evaluation through their state’s EI program so their child may be enrolled in EI and receive therapy services during the child’s first three years of life. Participants noted that despite many EI programs being required to plan for a child’s service transition as they approach age three, EI programs can no longer provide children services once they turn three. Participants further described how children may be less likely to receive diagnostic services if they are in EI because they are receiving needed therapy services and EI does not necessarily refer for or provide autism evaluation. Moreover, because many insurance plans require documentation of an autism diagnosis to cover autism-specific therapy services, such as ABA therapy, children may enter an indefinite interim period without services once they age out of EI. A participant elaborated as follows: “[S]o to give you an example, if there’s a suspicion of a developmental disability or autism at say two years four months, normally someone would enter- a child would enter the early intervention system and there would be a recommendation from either the child’s pediatrician or someone in the eye that this child obtains a neuro-psych for testing to determine if there is a diagnosis of autism. What’s happening now is it’s taking families up to a year to get to see someone. So, what happens is they transition out of early intervention before they’ve ever had an assessment. So, the child transitions to insurance at age three without an official diagnosis and the family can’t access any services.”(Participant 38, Massachusetts) Participants explained that children in EI often transition to the early childhood special education (ECSE) system once they turn three years old. Through ECSE, children can undergo an autism educational disability eligibility evaluation to receive services provided by their school’s special education program. However, challenges accessing an educational autism diagnosis – particularly through certain ECSE programs – are viewed as impeding children who have not already received a medical autism diagnosis from accessing home- and/or clinic-based therapy services.

#### Theme 4.

Persistent disparities in early autism diagnosis pathways are affected by regulations, procedures, actions, and practices within and between states. Within this theme, three subthemes emerged. Across these subthemes, participants discussed the influence of bias due to the cultural, linguistic, socioeconomic, geographic, functioning, and gender characteristics of children and their families. Participants frequently attributed these characteristics including their intersections (e.g., racial/ethnic minority groups living in rural areas) as contributing to persistent early autism diagnosis inequities. Member-checking interview findings generally affirmed this theme and its three subthemes.

##### Subtheme 4a. Developmental screening disparities.

Developmental screening disparities were described by participants as the most pronounced amongst children from diverse racial and ethnic groups and families with limited English proficiency. Participants attributed these disparities to the most widely used developmental screening tools not always being readily available in languages beyond English. Participants further explained how autism diagnostic practices commonly utilize a Eurocentric approach, creating challenges for culturally and linguistically diverse families. Participants additionally described how a lack of cultural concordance between diagnosticians and families can interfere with families’ accessing or following through with diagnostic services. That is, diagnosticians who do not share the same cultural identity as children and their families may be more likely to adopt a “wait-and-see” approach, minimizing families’ concerns due to diagnosticians’ inability to understand how autism may be differently recognized in diverse communities. This may also involve diagnosticians labeling a child’s autism symptomatology as behavioral or providing differential diagnoses (e.g., ADHD). Relatedly, several participants who provide autism diagnostic services in tribal communities acknowledged how autism and disability generally may be viewed differently, or not acknowledged at all, influencing early autism diagnosis for some Indigenous children.

> “Culturally, it’s also – since I do both – and the Hispanic culture, both of those groups, there’s often an unwillingness to have a diagnosis. I’ll tell you, particularly on Hopi and Navajo, having a child who has something that you recognize is different often is thought of as this child is very special and a shaman. Giving a diagnosis that seems to be critical is not acceptable. When I am on Navajo or Hopi and I’m giving a diagnosis, I don’t actually give a diagnosis, which kind of sounds weird. I don’t give a diagnosis because I know that culturally that won’t be acceptable. Generally, what I’ll do is tell a story about other children I’ve known who didn’t talk, and this is what this family did, and the child started talking. I don’t want to talk about changing the child because that would not be culturally acceptable.”
> 
> 
> (Participant 8, Arizona)

##### Subtheme 4b. Biases in autism diagnostic tools.

Participants explained how some autism diagnostic tools were not developed for use with diverse groups of children and families (e.g., children whose parents have limited English proficiency). Children from these populations may be less likely to receive early autism diagnosis due to a lack of culturally responsive diagnostic practices, their own cultural beliefs about disability, and biases that clinicians may have. As one participant described:

> “I think we can do a lot of ADOS’ in English, but […] when you have someone who […] speaks Spanish, it’s just a lot more difficult. It’s a lot more difficult to do a lot of their evaluation if they speak a different language.”
> 
> 
> (Participant 5, California)

##### Subtheme 4c. Usage of telemedicine in rural areas.

Participants described how children in rural, geographically isolated areas may be less likely to receive an early autism diagnosis due to a limited quantity of diagnostic resources and transportation challenges. The increased use of telemedicine spurred by the COVID-19 pandemic served to connect some geographically isolated families to autism diagnostic and treatment services. However, the effectiveness of telemedicine in these areas could be limited by poor internet connection.

## Discussion

This is one of the first and largest studies to explore policy factors influencing early autism diagnosis in the United States. Four overarching themes including developmental monitoring and screening, multiple factors shaping autism diagnostic pathways, EI programs affecting early diagnosis, and persistent early diagnosis disparities were identified. Aligned with previous research (Daniels & Mandell, 2014; Smith et al., 2024), this study’s results provide insights into policy driving state variation in the average age of autism diagnosis.

Despite national guidelines, this study’s results reinforce inconsistencies within and between states in how developmental monitoring and screening including autism-specific screening are approached (e.g., use of repeated screening, which screening tools are used) (Hirai et al., 2018; Wallis et al., 2020). Federal mandates requiring and incentivizing developmental monitoring and screening may help to standardize their use in medical, childcare, and early childhood education settings (Kogan et al., 2008; Rosenberg et al., 2016). The effective implementation of such policy would need to be supported by organizational and provider training to increase developmental screening and monitoring – particularly in certain settings (e.g., childcare) where developmental screening may not routinely occur. Past research has shown that these training programs are effective in increasing autism screening and assessment for young children (Choueiri et al., 2021). Similarly, repeated screening models shown to increase autism assessment in primary care could be more widely used and extended in childcare and early childhood education settings (Carbone et al., 2016; Dai et al., 2020).

Long wait times from parent and provider concerns about a child’s development to autism diagnosis are well established as contributing to late diagnosis, as well as poor access to evidence-based services (Zuckerman et al., 2015, 2017). This study’s results on diagnostic pathways shed further light on why early diagnosis often does not occur including shortages of professionals approved to diagnose autism within states, insurance plan requirements that certain assessment tools (e.g., ADOS-2) be used to verify the clinical need for specific services, and low Medicaid reimbursement rates for autism assessment disincentivizing health systems and providers to diagnose Medicaid enrolled children and making families of Medicaid-enrolled children less likely to pursue diagnosis due to steep out-of-pocket costs. Expanding the range of providers authorized to diagnose autism can help alleviate workforce shortages without compromising diagnostic reliability and accuracy (Barbaresi et al., 2022; McNally Keehn et al., 2020). Along these lines, providing greater incentives to providers who are authorized to diagnose autism across most states (e.g., DBPs) through greater loan repayment and higher salaries may help increase the workforce (Baum et al., 2024). A severity-based or “fast track” approach for triaging children with clinically evident and unmistakable autism symptomatology for immediate evaluation could also shorten wait times for children (de Marchena & Miller, 2017).

The agency of EI and other early childhood programs in early autism diagnosis was also highlighted in this study. Autism screening in EI is associated with increased autism diagnosis and disparities therein (Sheldrick et al., 2022). Still, states vary widely in which diagnosed conditions qualify children for EI services and what types of evaluations are undertaken for children in EI (Barger et al., 2019; Barton et al., 2016; Stahmer & Mandell, 2007; Williams et al., 2021). For instance, provisional “at-risk” for autism diagnoses by some EI programs can enable autism therapy services access for young children (Rotholz et al., 2017). Yet the disconnect between EI and subsequent services due to the requirement for a medical autism diagnosis to access services beyond EI can create a “service cliff” for some young children (Gordon-Lipkin et al., 2016). For these reasons, state EI programs may benefit from policies requiring universal autism screening and building diagnostic capacity to assess children identified as being at-risk before they transition.

Study findings reinforce the persistence of disparities in early autism diagnosis and provide additional insights into policy factors that may drive these disparities. Limited autism awareness and acceptance in certain communities were described by study participants and have been previously established (Lindly et al., 2023; Zuckerman et al., 2018) suggesting autism education and related programming are needed and should be culturally tailored (Lee et al., 2022). Notably, a body of research on the psychometric properties of the M-CHAT amongst racial minority populations demonstrates that child race/ethnicity and total M-CHAT score are not significantly associated (Dai et al., 2021; Guthrie et al., 2019; Khowaja et al., 2015; Scarpa et al., 2013), suggesting disparities in early autism identification may arise from other factors such as provider biases, diagnostic practices that are culturally incongruent, and language barriers. For these reasons, policy further advancing culturally, and linguistically concordant diagnostic processes including the provision of interpreters and translated assessment reports for families with limited English proficiency remains paramount. The more widespread use of biomarker-based autism assessments (e.g., eye tracking) may also help to reduce early diagnosis disparities.

### Strengths and Limitations

The study’s primary strength lies in its qualitative approach with a relatively large sample, which allowed for an in-depth exploration of many perspectives regarding policy contributing to early autism diagnosis. The involvement of community members, such as parents and autistic individuals, through interviews and member-checking further strengthens the credibility and utility of the study findings. Still, this study has limitations. First, the primary focus was on policy related to autism diagnosis, rather than extensively exploring policy related to behavioral therapy and other autism services. We also did not assess inter-rater reliability by computing statistics (e.g., Kappa coefficient) in checking consistency among team members while coding. Nevertheless, a post-hoc coding comparison across all codes pertinent to the final themes and subthemes showed good to fair agreement (mean Kappa = 0.73, mean coding agreement = 98.85%, mean coding disagreement = 1.15%; NVivo, n.d.). Additionally, most participants collectively represented five states, leaving more to be understood about policy driving early autism diagnosis in other states and across all states. Furthermore, there may be further variation from region to region within the states that were represented in this study beyond what we were able to capture. Gaps in participants’ knowledge about policy and other contextual factors that could influence the diagnostic process may also bias this study’s findings.

## Conclusion

Early autism diagnosis is critical to ensuring that children in the United States can access evidence-based services and supports thereby optimizing their health trajectories. This qualitative investigation provides new evidence on policies that drive barriers and facilitators to early autism diagnosis, and that vary geographically across the country. Policy factors and recommendations to increase early autism diagnosis overall and reduce disparities therein were identified related to developmental screening and monitoring, the autism diagnostic pathway, the role of early intervention and other early childhood programs, and persistent early autism diagnosis disparities. These findings may be used to help quantify, further understand, and intervene with policy to ultimately advance health equity for U.S. children with autism.

## _Abstract_

**Problem/Condition:**Autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

**Period Covered:**2022.

**Description of System:**The Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network is an active surveillance program that estimates prevalence and characteristics of ASD and monitors timing of ASD identification among children aged 4 and 8 years. In 2022, a total of 16 sites (located in Arizona, Arkansas, California, Georgia, Indiana, Maryland, Minnesota, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Tennessee, Texas [two sites: Austin and Laredo], Utah, and Wisconsin) conducted surveillance for ASD among children aged 4 and 8 years and suspected ASD among children aged 4 years. Surveillance included children who lived in the surveillance area at any time during 2022. Children were classified as having ASD if they ever received 1) an ASD diagnostic statement in a comprehensive developmental evaluation, 2) autism special education eligibility, or 3) an ASD _International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision_ (ICD-9) code in the 299 range or _International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision_ (ICD-10) code of F84.0, F84.3, F84.5, F84.8, or F84.9. Children aged 4 years were classified as having suspected ASD if they did not meet the case definition for ASD but had an evaluator’s suspicion of ASD documented in a comprehensive developmental evaluation.

**Results:**Among children aged 8 years in 2022, ASD prevalence was 32.2 per 1,000 children (one in 31) across the 16 sites, ranging from 9.7 in Texas (Laredo) to 53.1 in California. The overall observed prevalence estimate was similar to estimates calculated using Bayesian hierarchical and random effects models. ASD was 3.4 times as prevalent among boys (49.2) than girls (14.3). Overall, ASD prevalence was lower among non-Hispanic White (White) children (27.7) than among Asian or Pacific Islander (A/PI) (38.2), American Indian or Alaska Native (AI/AN) (37.5), non-Hispanic Black or African American (Black) (36.6), Hispanic or Latino (Hispanic) (33.0), and multiracial children (31.9). No association was observed between ASD prevalence and neighborhood median household income (MHI) at 11 sites; higher ASD prevalence was associated with lower neighborhood MHI at five sites.

Record abstraction was completed for 15 of the 16 sites for 8,613 children aged 8 years who met the ASD case definition. Of these 8,613 children, 68.4% had a documented diagnostic statement of ASD, 67.3% had a documented autism special education eligibility, and 68.9% had a documented ASD ICD-9 or ICD-10 code. All three elements of the ASD case definition were present for 34.6% of children aged 8 years with ASD.

Among 5,292 (61.4% of 8,613) children aged 8 years with ASD with information on cognitive ability, 39.6% were classified as having an intellectual disability. Intellectual disability was present among 52.8% of Black, 50.0% of AI/AN, 43.9% of A/PI, 38.8% of Hispanic, 32.7% of White, and 31.2% of multiracial children with ASD. The median age of earliest known ASD diagnosis was 47 months and ranged from 36 months in California to 69.5 months in Texas (Laredo).

Cumulative incidence of ASD diagnosis or eligibility by age 48 months was higher among children born in 2018 (aged 4 years in 2022) than children born in 2014 (aged 8 years in 2022) at 13 of the 15 sites that were able to abstract records. Overall cumulative incidence of ASD diagnosis or eligibility by age 48 months was 1.7 times as high among those born in 2018 compared with those born in 2014 and ranged from 1.4 times as high in Arizona and Georgia to 3.1 times as high in Puerto Rico. Among children aged 4 years, for every 10 children meeting the case definition of ASD, one child met the definition of suspected ASD.

Children with ASD who were born in 2018 had more evaluations and identification during ages 0–4 years than children with ASD who were born in 2014 during the 0–4 years age window, with an interruption in the pattern in early 2020 coinciding with onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Overall, 66.5% of children aged 8 years with ASD had a documented autism test. Use of autism tests varied widely across sites: 24.7% (New Jersey) to 93.5% (Puerto Rico) of children aged 8 years with ASD had a documented autism test in their records. The most common tests documented for children aged 8 years were the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Autism Spectrum Rating Scales, Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Gilliam Autism Rating Scale, and Social Responsiveness Scale.

**Interpretation:**Prevalence of ASD among children aged 8 years was higher in 2022 than previous years. ASD prevalence was higher among A/PI, Black, and Hispanic children aged 8 years than White children aged 8 years, continuing a pattern first observed in 2020. A/PI, Black, and Hispanic children aged 8 years with ASD were also more likely than White or multiracial children with ASD to have a co-occurring intellectual disability. Identification by age 48 months was higher among children born in 2018 compared with children born in 2014, suggesting increased early identification consistent with historical patterns.

**Public Health Action:**Increased identification of autism, particularly among very young children and previously underidentified groups, underscores the increased demand and ongoing need for enhanced planning to provide equitable diagnostic, treatment, and support services for all children with ASD. The substantial variability in ASD identification across sites suggests opportunities to identify and implement successful strategies and practices in communities to ensure all children with ASD reach their potential.

Top

## Introduction

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a developmental disability characterized by difficulties with social interaction or communication and the presence of restricted interests or repetitive behaviors. ASD is recognized as a heterogenous condition with wide variation in the type and severity of signs, symptoms, and levels of support needed among persons with ASD (_1_). In addition to developmental surveillance, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that pediatric care providers screen all children for ASD at ages 18 and 24 months (_2_,_3_). Additional screening might be needed if a child is at high risk for ASD or if signs and symptoms are present. Early identification of ASD can help children receive services and supports they might need for their development and to improve long-term outcomes (_4_).

The Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network has reported biennial ASD estimates among children aged 8 years since 2000. Prevalence increased from one in 150 in 2000 (_5_) to one in 36 in 2020 (_6_), and demographic patterns in ASD identification changed. Before 2016, the highest ASD prevalence was observed among White children and in children from neighborhoods with higher socioeconomic status (SES) (_7_). In 2020, higher ASD prevalence was observed for the first time among historically underserved groups including non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic children, and an association between ASD prevalence and SES (measured by median household income [MHI] tertile) was not present in the majority of sites (_6_).

The ADDM Network began tracking ASD among children aged 4 years in 2010 as an indicator of early identification of ASD (_8_). Although prevalence has been lower among children aged 4 years than aged 8 years in each reporting year, comparing cumulative incidence of identification by age 48 months has consistently indicated higher rates of ASD identification in younger cohorts (i.e., children born more recently) (_9_–_11_). A report that presented data collected in 2020 found interruptions to early identification during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic (_11_).

This report includes data from the expansion of the ADDM Network to 16 communities across the United States monitoring children aged 4 and 8 years with ASD in 2022. The ADDM Network began its sixth funding cycle in January 2023 with 11 sites; five additional sites were able to join in April because of 2023 Consolidated Appropriations Act (_12_) funds for expansion.

This report describes prevalence and characteristics of children with ASD as well as patterns in early ASD identification. These data can be used by communities to monitor trends, anticipate and understand service needs, and support efforts to ensure early and equitable identification of children with ASD.

Top

## Methods

### Surveillance Sites and Procedures

ADDM Network sites in Arizona, Arkansas, California, Georgia, Indiana, Maryland, Minnesota, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Tennessee, Texas (two sites: Austin and Laredo), Utah, and Wisconsin selected a geographic area of their state to conduct surveillance of ASD among children aged 4 and 8 years and surveillance of suspected ASD among children aged 4 years in 2022. All sites functioned as public health authorities under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 Privacy Rule and met applicable local institutional review board, privacy, and confidentiality requirements under 45 CFR Part 46. Sites also functioned as authorized representatives of Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) agencies to access education records under Family Education Rights and Privacy Act and IDEA consistent with 34 CFR Section 99.35.

### Case Ascertainment and Surveillance Case Definition

Surveillance was conducted using the same surveillance methods and case definitions used in 2018 and 2020 (_6_,_13_). To identify children with ASD, site personnel requested and linked records from health sources and education sources. All sites participating in 2022 had access to health and education records (Table 1). _International Classification of Diseases_ (ICD), _Ninth Revision_ (ICD-9) or ICD-10 developmental disability diagnosis codes were requested from health sources, which included service providers conducting developmental evaluations and state administrative programs. California, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Utah, and Wisconsin had access to state-funded disability services programs or Medicaid claims data. Special education eligibility data were requested from education sources. Thirteen sites had data agreements in place with education sources covering 100% of their study areas; three sites had agreements with education data sources covering <100% (Georgia [97.3%], Missouri [68.0%], and Texas [Laredo] [99.7%]). California, Maryland, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Utah, and Wisconsin had access to IDEA Part C early intervention data. Certain data sources (e.g., Medicaid) are administrative in nature and did not have physical or electronic records such as developmental evaluations available for review. Indiana had access only to special education eligibility category data from its educational source and ICD codes from its medical source. Therefore, Indiana was not included in analyses or visualizations of elements of the ASD case definition because information about ASD diagnostic statements was not available.

For this report, children aged 8 years (born in 2014) or aged 4 years (born in 2018) met the surveillance ASD case definition if they lived in the surveillance area at any time in 2022 and they received 1) an ASD diagnostic statement in a comprehensive developmental evaluation, 2) autism special education eligibility, or 3) an ASD ICD-9 code in the 299 range or ICD-10 code of F84.0, F84.3, F84.5, F84.8, or F84.9. Children aged 4 years were classified as having suspected ASD if they did not meet the criteria for ASD but had an evaluator’s suspicion of ASD documented in a comprehensive developmental evaluation. Additional demographic information, comprehensive developmental evaluations, individualized education programs (IEPs), scores from intelligence quotient (IQ) assessments, and presence of ASD diagnostic tests and assessment tools (tests) were collected from records for children.

### Additional Data Sources and Variable Definitions

The numbers of children aged 4 and 8 years living in each surveillance area were obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau Vintage 2022 county-level single-year-of-age postcensal population estimates for 2022 ([https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/technical-documentation/methodology.html](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/technical-documentation/methodology.html)). Surveillance areas at four sites (Arizona, California, Minnesota, and Texas [Austin]) were partial counties and were defined using census tracts. For these sites, postcensal population estimates were adjusted using American Community Survey (ACS) estimates of included census tracts (_14_). Full details are available (Supplementary Methods 1 and Supplementary Table 1, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)).

When information on race and ethnicity or sex was missing from records, birth certificate data were used if available. Co-occurring intellectual disability was defined as an IQ score of ≤70 or an examiner’s statement of intellectual disability on the child’s most recent IQ test. Evaluation by age 36 months was calculated using the earliest recorded developmental evaluation for each child. Earliest age at identification was defined as the child’s age in months at first recorded ASD diagnosis or special education eligibility (identification ages for children with only an ICD code were not available). Children were linked at the census tract level to socioeconomic indicators of neighborhood MHI from the 2022 ACS 5-year estimates (_14_) and CDC’s social vulnerability index (SVI) (_15_).

### Analytic Methods

ASD prevalence among children aged 8 years was calculated as the number of children who met the ASD surveillance case definition per 1,000 children of that age living in the surveillance area; ASD prevalence among children aged 4 years was calculated similarly. A Bayesian hierarchical modelling approach and random-effects restricted maximum likelihood method were also used to calculate overall prevalence and measures of uncertainty (95% Bayesian credible intervals and 95% CIs, respectively) among children aged 8 years to better account for the wide range in prevalence across sites; full details are available (Supplementary Methods 2, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Prevalence was calculated by sex and by race and ethnicity for American Indian or Alaska Native (AI/AN), Asian or Pacific Islander (A/PI), non-Hispanic Black (Black), non-Hispanic White (White), multiracial (two or more races), and Hispanic or Latino (Hispanic) children. Children of Hispanic origin of any race were categorized as Hispanic; all other racial groups were categorized as non-Hispanic. Children lacking information on sex (n = 13 children aged 8 years) or race and ethnicity (n = 106 children aged 4 years and 115 children aged 8 years) were excluded from analyses stratified by those variables. The U.S. Census Bureau’s Population Estimates Program does not include race and Hispanic origin detail for Puerto Rico at the municipio (municipality) level. Of the overall Puerto Rico population, 99% is Hispanic (_16_); for this analysis, children aged 4 and 8 years in Puerto Rico were considered Hispanic. Denominators for prevalence were therefore not available for cases with non-Hispanic ethnicity (n = 4 children aged 4 years and n = 2 children aged 8 years) reported by Puerto Rico.

Census tracts for all sites combined were grouped into low, medium, and high tertiles for MHI that included roughly equal populations of children in each respective age group. For children aged 8 years, the low tertile included neighborhoods with MHI up to $62,470, medium tertile up to $97,768, and high tertile up to $250,001. SVI data were grouped into low, medium, and high tertiles based on national percentile. Prevalence of ASD calculated by MHI and SVI tertile used the appropriate ACS 5-year population denominator (population of group aged 5–9 years divided by five to estimate a single year of age) for census tracts included in each tertile.

Prevalence estimates with a relative standard error ≥30% were suppressed because of limited statistical precision. Prevalence ratios were used to compare prevalence by sex and by race and ethnicity; prevalence ratios involving at least one suppressed estimate were likewise suppressed.

Because Indiana did not have data available from record abstraction, Indiana is included in analyses of prevalence (by demographic characteristics, MHI, and SVI) but excluded from other analyses that required data from record abstraction (e.g., co-occurring intellectual disability or presence of evaluation or diagnosis or age at evaluation or diagnosis).

Cumulative incidence of ASD per 1,000 children was calculated separately for children aged 4 and 8 years in 2022 by dividing the total number of children with earliest ASD diagnosis or eligibility at each month of age by the population denominator for children aged 4 years or 8 years in 2022. Cumulative incidence of diagnosis or eligibility by age 48 months was compared between children born in 2018 (aged 4 years in 2022) and those born in 2014 (aged 8 years in 2022) using risk ratios.

To assess the effect of potential service disruption during the COVID-19 pandemic on patterns of evaluation and identification, numbers of evaluations and identifications were aggregated by calendar month for children aged 4 and 8 years in 2022. To compare the same age windows (age 0–4 years) by calendar month, the numbers of evaluations and incidence of identification per 1,000 children from 2014 (year 0) through 2018 (year 4) for children aged 8 years was subtracted from the same months during 2018 (year 0) through 2022 (year 4) for children aged 4 years.

The Wilson score method was used to calculate 95% CIs for prevalence, prevalence ratios, prevalence differences, cumulative incidence, and risk ratios. Prevalence and risk ratios were considered significant when 95% CIs did not include 1.0. Prevalence differences (comparing 2020 and 2022 for sites participating in both years) were considered significant when 95% CIs did not include 0. The male-to-female prevalence ratio was compared among sites using the Mantel-Haenszel test of homogeneity. Cochran-Armitage tests of trend were used to assess trends across MHI and SVI tertiles when data were available for all tertiles. Pearson chi-square tests were used to compare differences in distributions between groups for analyses of co-occurring intellectual disability and evaluation by age 36 months. Mantel-Haenszel, Cochran-Armitage tests of trend, and chi-square tests were considered significant when the p value was <0.05. R software (version 4.4.1; R Foundation) was used for data analysis and visualization.

## Results

### ASD Prevalence Among Children Aged 8 Years

The overall observed ASD prevalence was 32.2 per 1,000 (one in 31) children aged 8 years and ranged from 9.7 in Texas (Laredo) to 53.1 in California (Table 1). The overall ASD prevalence using the Bayesian hierarchical modelling approach was 32.2 (95% Bayesian credible interval = 25.4–39.3) per 1,000 children aged 8 years; with the random-effects restricted maximum likelihood method it was 30.9 (95% CI = 25.8–36.0) per 1,000 children aged 8 years (Supplementary Methods 2, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Eleven sites also conducted ASD surveillance in 2020; estimates and differences in site boundaries or access to data sources are available (Supplementary Table 2, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Among the 11 sites, prevalence was higher in 2022 than in 2020 at nine (from 14.0% to 36.7% higher) and overall (22.2% higher [absolute difference of 6.1 more children with ASD per 1,000 children aged 8 years]). Prevalence was similar between 2020 and 2022 at two sites (Arizona and Utah). Further limiting the comparison to the five sites where site boundaries and data sources were the same between years, the absolute increase in ASD prevalence from 2020 to 2022 was still 6.1 per 1,000 children aged 8 years (22.8% higher) (Supplementary Table 2, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)).

The overall male-to-female prevalence ratio was 3.4, with overall ASD prevalence of 49.2 per 1,000 among boys and 14.3 per 1,000 among girls (Table 2). Evidence of heterogeneity of the male-to-female ratio was observed across sites (Table 2). ASD prevalence among children aged 8 years differed by racial and ethnic groups (calculated as ratios with White children, observed to have the lowest prevalence, as the reference group) (Table 2); prevalence ratios for additional comparisons of racial and ethnic groups are presented (Supplementary Table 3, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Prevalence among White children (27.7) was lower than prevalence among multiracial (31.9), Hispanic (33.0), Black (36.6), AI/AN (37.5), or A/PI children (38.2). Utah was the only site in which another racial or ethnic group had lower ASD prevalence than White children (multiracial compared with White).

For 11 sites, ASD prevalence was not associated with neighborhood MHI, but lower neighborhood MHI was associated with higher ASD prevalence for five sites (New Jersey, Tennessee, Texas [Laredo], Utah, and Wisconsin) and overall (although the overall trend was not monotonic) (Figure 1) (Supplementary Table 4, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Findings using SVI were generally similar: an association between SVI and ASD prevalence was not present at 11 sites and higher social vulnerability was observed with higher ASD prevalence at five sites (Maryland, New Jersey, Tennessee, Utah, and Wisconsin) and overall (although overall, Maryland and Tennessee trends were not monotonic) (Supplementary Figure 1, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)).

### Presence of ASD Diagnostic Statements, Special Education Eligibility, and ICD Codes Among Children Aged 8 Years

The percentage of children with diagnostic statements, special education eligibility, and ICD codes varied by site (Supplementary Tables 5 and 6, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Among the 15 sites that completed record abstraction, the percentage of children with ASD who had a documented ASD diagnostic statement was 68.4% overall (range=41.2% in Texas [Austin] to 95.0% in Puerto Rico) (Supplementary Table 5, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). ASD prevalence per 1,000 children aged 8 years based exclusively on documented ASD diagnostic statements was 22.5 overall (range=6.2 in Texas [Laredo] to 42.3 in California) (Figure 2) (Supplementary Table 6, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). The overall percentage of children with ASD who had a documented autism special education eligibility was 67.3% (range=38.3% in Texas [Laredo] to 90.2% in Puerto Rico) (Supplementary Table 5, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). The percentage of children with ASD who had a documented ICD code was 68.9% (range = 40.9% [Maryland] to 88.7% [Pennsylvania]). A majority (69.9%) of children with ASD had at least two of the three types of ASD identification documented in their records and 34.7% had all three types (Figure 3). Of 5,933 children with an ICD code, 86.3% also had a documented ASD diagnostic statement or autism special education eligibility; among all 8,613 children with ASD in the 15 sites that completed record abstraction, 9.4% met the case definition through having only an ICD code.

Categories of special education eligibility in children’s most recent IEPs varied by site; certain sites are in states that only use primary eligibility categories, whereas other sites also have information on secondary eligibility (Supplementary Table 7, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Of children with ≥1 IEP available in their records (63.7% of children aged 8 years), the top five eligibility categories were autism (77.7% of children); speech or language impairment (24.7%); health, physical, or other disability (7.9%); developmental delay (6.9%); and intellectual disability (3.6%).

### Cognitive Ability Among Children with ASD Aged 8 Years

Data on cognitive ability were available for 5,292 (61.4%) children aged 8 years with ASD (range = 21.3% in Texas [Laredo] to 90.2% in Arkansas) (Table 3). Similar percentages of girls and boys with ASD had data on cognitive ability (61.0 and 61.7%, respectively). Black children were less likely to have data on cognitive ability (59.3%) than multiracial children (66.4%) and White children (63.1%). The median age of most recent cognitive test was 67 months overall and varied by site (range = 45 months in Texas [Austin] to 85 months in Puerto Rico) (Table 3). Among children aged 8 years with ASD who had data on cognitive ability, 39.6% were classified as having intellectual disability (IQ ≤70) at their most recent test or examination, 24.2% were classified in the borderline range (IQ = 71–85), and 36.1% were classified in the average or higher range (IQ >85) (Table 3). The percentage of children with cognitive data available who were classified as having intellectual disability varied widely among sites (range = 24.8% in Puerto Rico to 80.0% in Texas [Laredo]). Overall, a similar proportion of girls and boys with ASD had intellectual disability (40.4% versus 39.5%, respectively). By race and ethnicity, Black children had a higher proportion of co-occurring intellectual disability (52.8%) than all other groups except AI/AN (50.0%) children. A/PI (43.9%) and Hispanic (38.8%) children had higher proportions of co-occurring intellectual disability than multiracial (31.2%) and White children (32.7%).

### Age at First Evaluation and ASD Diagnosis Among Children Aged 8 Years

Among 7,227 children aged 8 years with ASD and available evaluations, 50.3% were evaluated by age 36 months (range=42.2% in Missouri to 63.6% in Pennsylvania) (Table 4). Among the 5,887 children aged 8 years with ASD who had an evaluation containing an ASD diagnostic statement, the median age at earliest known diagnosis was 47 months (range = 36 months in California to 69.5 months in Texas [Laredo]) (Table 4). Children with ASD and intellectual disability had a lower median age at diagnosis (43 months) than children without an intellectual disability (49 months).

### Early ASD Identification Among Children Aged 4 and 8 Years

For 2022, prevalence per 1,000 children aged 4 years ranged from 12.9 (Indiana) to 60.6 (California) (Table 5) (Supplementary Figure 2, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). ASD prevalence per 1,000 children aged 4 years in the 16 sites combined was 29.3, which was 0.9 times the overall prevalence among children aged 8 years in 2022 (Table 5) (Supplementary Figure 3, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Overall prevalence among children aged 4 years was lower than among children aged 8 years in seven sites (Arizona, Arkansas, Georgia, Indiana, Minnesota, Missouri, and Utah), similar to children aged 8 years in four sites (Maryland, Pennsylvania, Texas [Austin], and Wisconsin), and higher than among children aged 8 years in five sites (California, New Jersey, Puerto Rico, Tennessee, and Texas [Laredo]).

Prevalence among children aged 4 years is also available by sex and race and ethnicity (Supplementary Table 8, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)), as is information about components of the case definition (Supplementary Figure 4, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Prevalence of suspected ASD was 3.1 per 1,000 children aged 4 years, which translated to one child suspected of having ASD for every 10 children identified with ASD among children aged 4 years (Supplementary Table 9 and Supplementary Figure 5, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)).

Children born in 2018 (aged 4 years in 2022) had 1.7 times the cumulative incidence of ASD diagnosis or eligibility by age 48 months as children born in 2014 (aged 8 years in 2022) (22.6 per 1,000 children compared with 13.1) (Figure 4) (Supplementary Table 10, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). This pattern was consistent at most (13 of 16) sites, ranging from 1.4 times as high in Arizona and Georgia to 3.1 times as high in Puerto Rico. Identification by age 48 months was similar between children born in 2014 and 2018 in Minnesota and Texas (Austin).

### Evaluation and Identification After COVID-19 Pandemic Onset

Children born in 2018 had more evaluations and ASD identifications than children born in 2014 when comparing the two groups of children for most months during the same age window (i.e., January 2018 through December 2022 for children aged 4 years in 2022 and January 2014 through December 2018 for children aged 8 years in 2022) (Figure 5). In March and April 2020, the first 2 months after the COVID-19 pandemic declaration, this pattern was disrupted, and the number of evaluations and rate of identification per 1,000 children was similar or lower for children born in 2018 compared with children born in 2014. The pattern of more evaluations and ASD identification among children born in 2018 resumed by June 2020 (Figure 5) and varied by site (Supplementary Figures 6 and 7, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)).

### ASD Testing Among Children Aged 4 and 8 Years

Autism testing practices varied among sites (Figure 6), ranging from 24.7% (New Jersey) to 93.5% (Puerto Rico) of children with ASD aged 8 years having any autism test documented in their records (Supplementary Table 11, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). Overall, 66.5% of children aged 8 years with ASD had any documented autism test. The most common autism tests were the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) (39.6% overall; range = 10.6%–63.9%), Autism Spectrum Rating Scales (ASRS) (30.2% overall; range = 0.3%–64.5%), Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) (24.1% overall; range = 10.1%–70.7%), Gilliam Autism Rating Scale (GARS) (12.2% overall; range = 1.4%–60.1%), Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS) (12.0­­­­­­­% overall; range = 0.3%–37.7%), and Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) (2.7% overall; range = 0%–11.6%). Compared with children aged 8 years with ASD, a similar proportion of children aged 4 years with ASD had an ASD test documented in their records (69.1%), though the order of tests by frequency was different (Supplementary Figure 8, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)). The most common autism test documented among children aged 4 years with ASD was the CARS (38.0%), followed by the ADOS (31.7%), ASRS (21.1%), TELE-ASD-PEDS (8.7%), SRS (8.1%), GARS (6.2%), and ADI-R (3.8%). ASD tests varied widely among children aged 4 years by site (Supplementary Figure 9, [https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/177099#tabs-3)).
